He meant to provide for me generously and believed he had done so. But when the parish became vacant, it was given to someone else."

16.32.oldText: "A deep, deliberate dislike of me—a dislike that I can only attribute in part to jealousy. Had the late Mr. Darcy liked me less, his son might have tolerated me better. But his father's extraordinary attachment to me irritated him, I believe, from a very early age. He did not have the temperament to bear the kind of rivalry between us—the kind of preference that was often shown to me."

16.36.oldText: Elizabeth was again deep in thought and after a time exclaimed, "To treat in such a way the godson, the friend, the favorite of his father!" She could have added, "A young man, too, like _you_, whose very face is proof of being good." But she contented herself with: "And someone who had probably been his companion from childhood, connected together, as I think you said, in the closest way."

16.39.oldText: "It _is_ remarkable," replied Wickham, "for almost everything he does can be traced to pride—and pride has often been his best quality. It has brought him closer to virtue than any other feeling. But none of us are consistent, and in his treatment of me there were impulses even stronger than pride."

16.55.oldText: "Her daughter, Miss de Bourgh, will have a very large fortune, and it is widely believed that she and her cousin will marry and unite the two estates."

16.56.oldText: This information made Elizabeth smile, as she thought of poor Miss Bingley. How useless all her attentions must be—useless her affection for his sister and her praise of himself—if he was already destined for another.

16.58.oldText: "I believe she is both, to a great degree," replied Wickham. "I have not seen her for many years, but I remember well that I never liked her and that her manner was domineering and rude. She has a reputation for being remarkably clever and intelligent, but I rather think she owes part of that reputation to her rank and fortune, part to her commanding manner, and the rest to the pride of her nephew, who insists that everyone connected with him should be considered first-rate."

16.59.oldText: Elizabeth agreed that he had given a very reasonable account of it, and they continued talking together with mutual enjoyment until supper ended the card games and gave the other ladies their share of Mr. Wickham's attention. There was no possibility of conversation in the noise of Mrs. Philips's supper party, but his manners recommended him to everyone. Whatever he said was said well, and whatever he did was done gracefully. Elizabeth left with her head full of him. She could think of nothing but Mr. Wickham and what he had told her all the way home. But there was no time to even mention his name on the journey, for neither Lydia nor Mr. Collins were silent for a moment. Lydia talked constantly about lottery tickets, about the money she had lost and won; and Mr. Collins, describing the politeness of Mr. and Mrs. Philips, insisting that he did not in the least mind his losses at whist, listing every dish at supper, and repeatedly worrying that he was crowding his cousins, had more to say than he could manage before the carriage stopped at Longbourn House.

17.0.oldText: The next day, Elizabeth told Jane what had passed between Mr. Wickham and herself. Jane listened with astonishment and concern—she could not believe that Mr. Darcy could be so unworthy of Mr. Bingley's friendship, and yet it was not in her nature to question the honesty of a young man as pleasant-looking as Wickham. The possibility that he had really suffered such cruelty was enough to touch all her tender feelings. Nothing remained, therefore, but to think well of them both, to defend each one's behavior, and to put down to accident or misunderstanding anything that could not otherwise be explained.

18.13.oldText: "Are you speaking for your own feelings in this case, or do you imagine you are pleasing mine?"

18.49.oldText: "No," replied Jane, "I have not forgotten him, but I have nothing satisfying to tell you. Mr. Bingley does not know his whole history and is quite unaware of the circumstances that have especially offended Mr. Darcy. But he will vouch for the good character, integrity, and honor of his friend, and is perfectly convinced that Mr. Wickham has deserved much less attention from Mr. Darcy than he has received. And I am sorry to say that by his account, as well as his sister's, Mr. Wickham is by no means a respectable young man. I'm afraid he has been very reckless and has deserved to lose Mr. Darcy's regard."

18.58.oldText: "Indeed I am. I shall beg his pardon for not having done it sooner. I believe him to be Lady Catherine's _nephew_. It will be in my power to assure him that her Ladyship was quite well a week ago Saturday."

18.62.oldText: Since Elizabeth no longer had any interest of her own to pursue, she turned her attention almost entirely to her sister and Mr. Bingley. The pleasant train of thought that her observations inspired made her perhaps nearly as happy as Jane. She pictured her sister settled in that very house, enjoying all the happiness that a marriage of true affection could bring, and she felt capable, under such circumstances, of even trying to like Bingley's two sisters. Her mother's thoughts were plainly running in the same direction, and she resolved not to go near her, for fear of hearing too much. When they sat down to supper, therefore, she considered it a most unfortunate coincidence that placed them within earshot of each other. She was deeply upset to find that her mother was talking freely and openly to Lady Lucas about nothing but her expectation that Jane would soon marry Mr. Bingley. It was a thrilling subject, and Mrs. Bennet seemed tireless in listing the advantages of the match. His being such a charming young man, and so rich, and living only three miles away were the first points of self-congratulation. Then it was such a comfort to think how fond the two sisters were of Jane, and to be certain they must want the connection as much as she did. It was, moreover, so promising for her younger daughters, since Jane's marrying so well would surely bring them into contact with other rich men. And lastly, it was so pleasant at her age to be able to hand her single daughters over to their sister's care, so that she need not go out in society more than she liked. It was necessary to present this as a matter of pleasure, because etiquette demanded it—but no one was less likely than Mrs. Bennet to find comfort in staying at home at any point in her life. She concluded with many good wishes that Lady Lucas might soon be equally fortunate—though obviously and triumphantly believing there was no chance of it.

18.66.oldText: Nothing she could say, however, had any influence. Her mother continued to broadcast her views at the same clearly audible volume. Elizabeth blushed and blushed again with shame and frustration. She could not help frequently glancing at Mr. Darcy, though every glance confirmed her fears—for though he was not always looking at her mother, she was sure his attention was invariably fixed on her. The expression on his face changed gradually from angry contempt to a composed and steady gravity.

18.74.oldText: The Longbourn party was the last to leave, and through a maneuver of Mrs. Bennet's had to wait for their carriage a quarter of an hour after everyone else had gone—which gave them time to see how eagerly some of the household wished them away. Mrs. Hurst and her sister barely opened their mouths except to complain of tiredness, and were obviously impatient to have the house to themselves. They rebuffed every attempt by Mrs. Bennet at conversation, casting a pall over the whole group that was scarcely lightened by the long speeches of Mr. Collins, who was complimenting Mr. Bingley and his sisters on the elegance of their party and the hospitality and politeness they had shown their guests. Darcy said nothing at all. Mr. Bennet, equally silent, was enjoying the scene. Mr. Bingley and Jane stood a little apart from the rest, talking only to each other. Elizabeth maintained as steady a silence as either Mrs. Hurst or Miss Bingley, and even Lydia was too tired to do more than occasionally exclaim "God, I'm so tired!" followed by a huge yawn.

19.21.oldText: To such stubbornness in willful self-deception Elizabeth would make no reply, and she immediately and silently left the room—determined that if he continued to interpret her repeated refusals as flattering encouragement, she would appeal to her father, whose rejection could be delivered in a manner that must be decisive, and whose behavior at least could not be mistaken for the flirtation of a sophisticated woman.

20.0.oldText: Mr. Collins was not left long to the quiet contemplation of his successful love, for Mrs. Bennet, who had been hovering in the hallway waiting for the conference to end, no sooner saw Elizabeth open the door and hurry past her toward the stairs than she entered the breakfast room and warmly congratulated both him and herself on the happy prospect of their closer connection. Mr. Collins received and returned these congratulations with equal pleasure, and proceeded to share the details of the conversation, with the result of which he had every reason to be satisfied—since his cousin's firm refusal would naturally come from her bashful modesty and the genuine delicacy of her character.

20.29.oldText: "Yes, there she comes," continued Mrs. Bennet, "looking as unconcerned as can be, and caring no more about us than if we were a hundred miles away, as long as she gets her own way. But I tell you what, Miss Lizzy—if you keep turning down every offer of marriage like this, you will never get a husband at all. And I am sure I don't know who is going to support you when your father is dead. _I_ won't be able to keep you—so I warn you. I am done with you from this very day. I told you in the library, you know, that I would never speak to you again, and you will find I keep my word. I have no pleasure in talking to disobedient children. Not that I have much pleasure in talking to anybody. People who suffer as I do from nervous complaints have no great desire for conversation. Nobody can imagine what I suffer! But it is always the same. Those who don't complain are never pitied."

21.2.oldText: After breakfast, the girls walked to Meryton to find out whether Mr. Wickham had returned and to lament his absence from the Netherfield ball. He met them as they entered town and accompanied them to their aunt's, where his regret and frustration, and everyone's concern, were thoroughly discussed. To Elizabeth, however, he privately admitted that his absence had been his own decision.

21.25.oldText: Elizabeth treated the idea of his not returning with utter contempt. It seemed to her nothing more than the product of Caroline's self-interested scheming, and she could not for a moment suppose that those wishes, however openly or cunningly expressed, could influence a young man so completely independent of everyone.

22.1.oldText: Charlotte assured her friend that she was happy to be helpful, and that it more than repaid her for the small sacrifice of her time. This was very kind—but Charlotte's purpose went further than Elizabeth had any idea. Her aim was nothing less than to prevent any return of Mr. Collins's attentions to Elizabeth by directing them toward herself. Such was Miss Lucas's plan, and appearances were so promising that when they parted that night, she would have felt almost sure of success if he had not been leaving Hertfordshire so soon. But here she underestimated the fire and independence of his character, for it led him to sneak out of Longbourn House the next morning with admirable stealth and hurry to Lucas Lodge to throw himself at her feet. He was anxious to avoid his cousins' notice, convinced that if they saw him leave they would surely guess his purpose, and he did not want the attempt known until its success was. Though he felt fairly confident—and with reason, for Charlotte had been reasonably encouraging—he was somewhat cautious after Wednesday's experience. His reception, however, was of the most flattering kind. Miss Lucas spotted him from an upstairs window as he walked toward the house and immediately set out to meet him "accidentally" in the lane. But she had hardly dared to hope that so much love and eloquence awaited her there.

22.2.oldText: In as short a time as Mr. Collins's long speeches would allow, everything was settled between them to the satisfaction of both. As they entered the house, he earnestly begged her to name the day that would make him the happiest of men. Though this request had to be put off for now, the lady felt no desire to play games with his happiness. The dullness that nature had bestowed on him would protect his courtship from any charm that could make a woman wish it to continue, and Miss Lucas, who accepted him purely from the practical and clear-headed desire for a stable home, did not care how soon that home was secured.

22.3.oldText: Sir William and Lady Lucas were quickly asked for their consent, which was given with the most joyful eagerness. Mr. Collins's current circumstances made it an excellent match for their daughter, to whom they could give little money, and his prospects for future wealth were extremely good. Lady Lucas immediately began to calculate, with more interest than the matter had ever

22.4.oldText: inspired before, how many years longer Mr. Bennet was likely to live. Sir William gave it as his firm opinion that whenever Mr. Collins came into possession of the Longbourn estate, it would be highly advisable for both him and his wife to be presented at the royal court. The whole family, in short, was suitably overjoyed. The younger girls began hoping they might be launched into society a year or two sooner than expected, and the boys were relieved of their fear that Charlotte would die an old maid. Charlotte herself was fairly calm. She had achieved her goal and had time to think about it. Her reflections were generally satisfactory. Mr. Collins, to be sure, was neither clever nor pleasant; his company was tedious, and his attachment to her must be imaginary. But he would still be her husband. Without thinking highly of either men or marriage, marriage had always been her goal. It was the only respectable option for well-educated young women with small fortunes, and however unlikely to bring happiness, it was their best protection against poverty. This protection she had now secured, and at twenty-seven, without ever having been pretty, she felt all the good fortune of it. The least pleasant aspect of the business was the surprise it would cause Elizabeth Bennet, whose friendship she valued above anyone else's. Elizabeth would be astonished, and would probably disapprove. And though her decision could not be shaken, her feelings would be hurt by such disapproval. She resolved to tell Elizabeth herself, and therefore instructed Mr. Collins, when he returned to Longbourn for dinner, to drop no hint of what had happened in front of the family. A promise of secrecy was of course dutifully given, but it could hardly be kept—for the curiosity aroused by his long absence erupted in such direct questions on his return that considerable ingenuity was needed to dodge them. At the same time, he was exercising great self-control, for he was desperate to announce his successful romance.

22.5.oldText: Since he had to begin his journey too early the next morning to see any of the family, the farewell ceremony was performed when the ladies retired for the night. Mrs. Bennet, with great politeness and warmth, said how happy they would be to see him at Longbourn again, whenever his other commitments allowed him to visit.

22.6.oldText: "My dear madam," he replied, "this invitation is particularly gratifying, because it is exactly what I have been hoping to receive. And you may be very certain that I shall take you up on it as soon as possible."

22.7.oldText: They were all astonished, and Mr. Bennet, who by no means wished for such a quick return, immediately said:

22.8.oldText: "But isn't there a danger of Lady Catherine disapproving, my good sir? You had better neglect your relatives than risk offending your patroness."

22.9.oldText: "My dear sir," replied Mr. Collins, "I am particularly grateful for this friendly warning, and you may count on my not taking so important a step without her Ladyship's approval."

22.10.oldText: "You cannot be too cautious. Risk anything rather than her displeasure. And if you think your coming to us again might provoke it—which I should think extremely likely—just stay quietly at home, and rest assured that _we_ shall take no offense."

22.11.oldText: "Believe me, my dear sir, my gratitude is warmly aroused by such affectionate concern. And rest assured, you will shortly receive from me a letter of thanks for this and for every other kindness shown during my stay in Hertfordshire. As for my fair cousins, though my absence may not be long enough to require it, I will now take the liberty of wishing them health and happiness—not excluding my cousin Elizabeth."

22.12.oldText: With proper goodbyes, the ladies then withdrew, all equally surprised to learn that he was planning a quick return. Mrs. Bennet liked to think he meant to propose to one of her younger girls, and Mary might have been persuaded to accept him. She rated his abilities much higher than any of the others did—there was a substance to his thoughts that often struck her—and though by no means as clever as herself, she thought that if encouraged to read and improve himself by her example, he might become a very agreeable companion. But the following morning put an end to all such hopes. Miss Lucas called soon after breakfast and, in a private conversation with Elizabeth, told her what had happened the day before.

22.13.oldText: The possibility that Mr. Collins might fancy himself in love with her friend had occurred to Elizabeth in the last day or two. But that Charlotte would encourage him seemed almost as impossible as encouraging him herself, and her astonishment was therefore so great that it at first broke through the bounds of good manners, and she could not help crying out:

22.14.oldText: "Engaged to Mr. Collins! My dear Charlotte—impossible!"

22.15.oldText: The composure that Miss Lucas had maintained while telling her story gave way to a momentary fluster at receiving so direct a reproach. But since it was no more than she expected, she soon recovered her calm and replied quietly:

22.16.oldText: "Why should you be surprised, my dear Eliza? Do you think it impossible that Mr. Collins could win any woman's good opinion, just because he was not lucky enough to succeed with you?"

22.17.oldText: But Elizabeth had collected herself, and with a strong effort was able to assure her, with reasonable steadiness, that the prospect of their closer relationship was very pleasing to her, and that she wished her every happiness imaginable.

22.18.oldText: "I see what you are feeling," replied Charlotte. "You must be surprised—very much surprised—since so recently Mr. Collins was wanting to marry you. But when you have had time to think it all over, I hope you will be satisfied with what I have done. I am not romantic, you know—I never was. I ask only for a comfortable home, and considering Mr. Collins's character, connections, and position, I am convinced that my chance of happiness with him is as good as most people can claim when they enter marriage."

22.19.oldText: Elizabeth quietly answered, "Of course," and after an awkward pause, they rejoined the rest of the family. Charlotte did not stay much longer, and Elizabeth was left to reflect on what she had heard. It was a long time before she became at all reconciled to the idea of such an unsuitable match. The strangeness of Mr. Collins making two proposals within three days was nothing compared to his actually being accepted. She had always known that Charlotte's views on marriage were not exactly like her own, but she could not have believed it possible that, when put to the test, Charlotte would sacrifice every finer feeling for worldly advantage. Charlotte, the wife of Mr. Collins, was a deeply humiliating picture! And to the pain of a friend disgracing herself and falling in her estimation was added the distressing certainty that it was impossible for that friend to be even tolerably happy with the choice she had made.

23.3.oldText: Elizabeth, feeling it was her duty to rescue him from this unpleasant situation, stepped forward to confirm his account by mentioning that she already knew about it from Charlotte herself. She tried to put a stop to her mother's and sisters' exclamations through her warm congratulations to Sir William—in which Jane readily joined—and by making various comments about the happiness the match would bring, Mr. Collins's excellent character, and the convenient distance of Hunsford from London.

23.15.oldText: Mrs. Bennet was really in a most pitiable state. The slightest mention of anything connected with the match threw her into a fit of bad temper, and wherever she went she was sure to hear it discussed. The sight of Miss Lucas was hateful to her. As her future successor in the house, she regarded Charlotte with jealous loathing. Whenever Charlotte came to visit, she assumed she was counting the hours until she took possession. And whenever Charlotte spoke in a low voice to Mr. Collins, she was convinced they were discussing the Longbourn estate and planning to turn her and her daughters out of the house as soon as Mr. Bennet died. She complained bitterly about all this to her husband.

24.2.oldText: Elizabeth, to whom Jane soon communicated the gist of all this, heard it in silent indignation. Her heart was divided between concern for her sister and resentment against everyone else. She gave no credit to Caroline's claim that her brother preferred Miss Darcy. That he was genuinely fond of Jane she doubted no more than she ever had. And much as she had always been inclined to like him, she could not think without anger—hardly without contempt—of his weak temperament and lack of proper resolve, which now made him the slave of his scheming friends and led him to sacrifice his own happiness to their whims. Had only his own happiness been at stake, he might have been free to play with it however he liked. But her sister's was involved too, and she felt he must know that. It was, in short, a subject on which she could reflect endlessly without getting anywhere. She could think of nothing else—and yet whether Bingley's feelings had truly faded, or were being suppressed by his friends' interference, whether he had known of Jane's attachment or it had escaped his notice—whichever was the case, though her opinion of him would be greatly affected by which it was, her sister's situation was the same, her peace equally damaged.

24.14.oldText: "And men make sure that it should."

24.22.oldText: "Your first assumption is wrong. They may wish for many things besides his happiness—they may wish for an increase in his wealth and status. They may wish him to marry a girl who has all the advantages of money, important connections, and social standing."

24.23.oldText: "There is no doubt they wish he would choose Miss Darcy," replied Jane. "But this may come from better motives than you suppose. They have known her much longer than they have known me—no wonder if they love her better. But whatever their own wishes may be, it is very unlikely they would have opposed their brother. What sister would think herself free to do so, unless something was seriously wrong? If they believed he was attached to me, they would not try to separate us. And if he were attached to me, they could not succeed. By imagining such a scenario, you make everyone behave unnaturally and wrongly, and me most unhappy. Don't distress me with the idea. I am not ashamed of having been mistaken—or at least, it is slight, nothing compared to what I would feel if I thought badly of him or his sisters. Let me see it in the best light—in the way it may be understood."

26.29.oldText: All this was shared with Mrs. Gardiner, and after describing the circumstances, she continued: "I am now convinced, my dear aunt, that I have never been deeply in love—for if I had really experienced that pure and powerful passion, I should at this moment detest his very name and wish him every kind of misfortune. But my feelings toward _him_ are not only friendly, they are even fair toward Miss King. I cannot find that I hate her at all, or that I am the least bit unwilling to think her a perfectly nice girl. There can be no love in all this. My vigilance has been effective. And though I would certainly be a more interesting figure to my acquaintances were I distractedly in love with him, I cannot say I regret my relative insignificance. Importance may sometimes be purchased too dearly. Kitty and Lydia take his defection much more to heart than I do. They are young in the ways of the world, and not yet open to the humbling truth that handsome young men must have something to live on, just like everyone else."

27.22.oldText: No plan could have been more appealing to Elizabeth, and her acceptance was immediate and grateful. "My dear, dear aunt," she cried rapturously, "what delight! What joy! You give me new life and energy. Goodbye to disappointment and gloom. What are men compared to rocks and mountains? Oh, what hours of bliss we shall have! And when we _do_ return, it will not be like other travelers, unable to describe a single thing accurately. We _will_ know where we have been—we _will_ remember what we have seen. Lakes, mountains, and rivers will not be jumbled together in our imaginations, and when we try to describe a particular scene, we will not start arguing about where it was. Let _our_ first impressions be less unbearable than those of the average tourist."

28.6.oldText: "Yes, Miss Elizabeth, you will have the honor of seeing Lady Catherine de Bourgh at church next Sunday, and I need not say you will be delighted with her. She is all friendliness and graciousness, and I have no doubt you will be honored with some share of her attention after the service. I have scarcely any hesitation in saying that she will include you and my sister Maria in every invitation with which she honors us during your stay here. Her behavior toward my dear Charlotte is charming. We dine at Rosings twice every week and are never allowed to walk home—her Ladyship's carriage is always sent for us. I _should_ say, one of her Ladyship's carriages, for she has several."

29.9.oldText: From the entrance hall—the fine proportions and finished details of which Mr. Collins pointed out with a rapturous air—they followed the servants through an anteroom to the room where Lady Catherine, her daughter, and Mrs. Jenkinson were sitting. Her Ladyship rose graciously to receive them. Since Mrs. Collins had arranged with her husband that the introductions would be her job, they were performed properly, without any of the apologies and thanks he would have considered necessary.

29.14.oldText: When the ladies returned to the drawing room, there was little to do but listen to Lady Catherine talk, which she did without pause until coffee arrived, delivering her opinion on every subject in so decisive a manner as showed she was not used to having her judgment questioned. She inquired into Charlotte's household matters in great detail and gave her a great deal of advice on managing everything. She told her how everything should be run in a household as small as hers and instructed her on the care of her cows and poultry. Elizabeth found that nothing was beneath this great lady's attention that could give her an opportunity to tell others what to do. In the breaks between her conversations with Mrs. Collins, she addressed various questions to Maria and Elizabeth, but especially to Elizabeth, about whom she knew the least, and who, she remarked to Mrs. Collins, was a very well-mannered, pretty sort of girl. She asked her at different times how many sisters she had, whether they were older or younger than herself, whether any of them were likely to marry, whether they were pretty, where they had been educated, what carriage her father kept, and what her mother's maiden name was. Elizabeth felt the full impertinence of her questions but answered them all calmly. Lady Catherine then observed:

29.37.oldText: Lady Catherine seemed quite astonished at not receiving a direct answer, and Elizabeth suspected she was the first person who had ever dared to trifle with such grand impertinence.

29.40.oldText: When the gentlemen had joined them and tea was over, the card tables were set up. Lady Catherine, Sir William, and Mr. and Mrs. Collins sat down to quadrille. Since Miss de Bourgh chose to play casino, the two girls had the honor of helping Mrs. Jenkinson make up her table. Their game was supremely dull. Scarcely a word was spoken that did not relate to the cards, except when Mrs. Jenkinson expressed her fears that Miss de Bourgh was too hot or too cold, or had too much or too little light. Much more happened at the other table. Lady Catherine was generally speaking—pointing out the other three players' mistakes or telling some story about herself. Mr. Collins was busy agreeing with everything her Ladyship said, thanking her for every hand he won, and apologizing if he thought he won too many. Sir William said little. He was storing up anecdotes and noble names in his memory.

30.2.oldText: Very few days passed without Mr. Collins walking over to Rosings, and not many without his wife feeling it necessary to do the same. Until Elizabeth remembered that there might be other parish appointments to be gained, she could not understand the sacrifice of so many hours. Now and then they were honored with a visit from her Ladyship, and nothing going on in the room escaped her observation during these calls. She examined their occupations, looked at their work, and told them to do it differently. She found fault with the furniture arrangement and caught the maid being negligent. And if she accepted any refreshment, she seemed to do so only to point out that Mrs. Collins's cuts of meat were too large for her family.

30.5.oldText: In this quiet way the first two weeks of her visit passed. Easter was approaching, and the week before it was to bring an addition to the family at Rosings—which in so small a circle must be important. Elizabeth had heard, soon after her arrival, that Mr. Darcy was expected there within a few weeks. And though there were not many of her acquaintances she did not prefer to him, his coming would provide a relatively new face at their Rosings parties, and she might be amused by seeing how hopeless Miss Bingley's pursuit of him was, judging by his behavior toward his cousin—the woman Lady Catherine had clearly destined for him. Lady Catherine talked of his coming with the greatest satisfaction, spoke of him in terms of the highest admiration, and seemed almost annoyed to learn that Miss Lucas and Elizabeth had already seen him several times.

30.6.oldText: His arrival was soon known at the parsonage, for Mr. Collins spent the whole morning walking within sight of the gates opening onto Hunsford Lane, in order to have

30.7.oldText: the earliest confirmation of it. After bowing as the carriage turned into the park, he hurried home with the great news. The following morning he rushed to Rosings to pay his respects. There were two nephews of Lady Catherine requiring them, for Mr. Darcy had brought with him a Colonel Fitzwilliam, the younger son of his uncle, a lord. And to the great surprise of the whole household, when Mr. Collins returned, the gentlemen came with him. Charlotte had seen them from her husband's study crossing the road, and immediately ran into the other room to tell the girls what an honor they could expect, adding:

30.8.oldText: "I may thank you, Eliza, for this courtesy. Mr. Darcy would never have come so soon to visit me."

30.9.oldText: Elizabeth had barely time to deny any claim to the compliment before their approach was announced by the doorbell, and shortly afterward the three gentlemen entered the room. Colonel Fitzwilliam, who led the way, was about thirty, not handsome, but in appearance and manner every inch the gentleman. Mr. Darcy looked just as he always had in Hertfordshire, paid his respects to Mrs. Collins with his usual reserve, and whatever his feelings toward her friend might be, greeted her with every appearance of composure. Elizabeth merely curtsied to him without saying a word.

30.10.oldText: Colonel Fitzwilliam struck up a conversation immediately, with the ease and confidence of a well-bred man, and talked very pleasantly. But his cousin, after making a brief remark about the house and garden to Mrs. Collins, sat for some time without speaking to anyone. At last, however, his politeness stirred enough for him to ask Elizabeth about the health of her family. She answered in the usual way, and after a moment's pause, added:

30.11.oldText: "My eldest sister has been in town these three months. Have you never happened to see her there?"

30.12.oldText: She knew perfectly well he never had, but she wanted to see whether he would betray any awareness of what had passed between the Bingleys and Jane. She thought he looked a little uncomfortable as he answered that he had never been fortunate enough to meet Miss Bennet. The subject was dropped, and the gentlemen soon left.

31.2.oldText: Colonel Fitzwilliam seemed genuinely glad to see them—anything was a welcome relief to him at Rosings—and Mrs. Collins's pretty friend had caught his eye considerably. He now sat beside her and talked so agreeably about Kent and Hertfordshire, about traveling and staying home, about new books and music, that Elizabeth had never been half so well entertained in that room before. They conversed with so much energy and flow that they drew the attention of Lady Catherine herself, as well as Mr. Darcy. _His_ eyes had been quickly and repeatedly turned toward them with a look of curiosity, and that her Ladyship eventually shared the feeling was more openly shown, for she did not hesitate to call out:

31.11.oldText: When coffee was over, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth that she had promised to play for him, and she sat down at the piano immediately. He drew a chair near her. Lady Catherine listened to half a song, then resumed talking to her other nephew—until Darcy walked away from her and, moving with his usual deliberation toward the piano, positioned himself so as to have a full view of the performer's face. Elizabeth saw what he was doing and, at the first convenient pause, turned to him with a knowing smile and said:

31.12.oldText: "You mean to frighten me, Mr. Darcy, by coming over in such state to listen. But I will not be intimidated, even though your sister _does_ play so well. There is a stubbornness in me that cannot bear to be scared by other people's wishes. My courage always rises with every attempt to bully me."

31.28.oldText: Elizabeth looked at Darcy to see how warmly he endorsed his cousin's praise, but neither at that moment nor at any other could she detect any sign of love. And from his whole manner toward Miss de Bourgh she drew this comfort for Miss Bingley: that he might just as easily have married _her_, had she been his relative.

32.23.oldText: Elizabeth looked surprised. The gentleman seemed to experience some change of feeling; he drew back his chair, picked up a newspaper from the table, and, glancing over it, said in a cooler voice:

33.0.oldText: More than once, Elizabeth unexpectedly ran into Mr. Darcy during her walks in the park. She felt the full perversity of the bad luck that should bring him where no one else came. To prevent it happening again, she took care to inform him at first that this was a favorite spot of hers. How it could happen a second time, therefore, was very strange! Yet it did—and even a third time. It seemed like deliberate bad luck or voluntary penance, for on these occasions it was not merely a few formal questions and an awkward pause before moving on—he actually thought it necessary to turn back and walk with her. He never said much, and she did not trouble herself to talk or listen much either. But during their third encounter, it struck her that he was asking some oddly disconnected questions—about whether she was enjoying Hunsford, her love of solitary walks, and her opinion of Mr. and Mrs. Collins's happiness. And in speaking of Rosings, and her not having fully explored the house, he seemed to assume that whenever she came to Kent again she would be staying _there_ too. His words seemed to imply it. Could he have Colonel Fitzwilliam in mind? She supposed, if he meant anything, he must be hinting at what might develop in that direction. It unsettled her a little, and she was quite glad to reach the gate opposite the parsonage.

34.1.oldText: She could not think of Darcy leaving Kent without remembering that his cousin would go with him. But Colonel Fitzwilliam had made it clear that he had no intentions at all, and agreeable as he was, she did not mean to be unhappy about him.

34.3.oldText: "I have struggled with this in vain. It will not do. My feelings will not be suppressed. You must allow me to tell you how deeply I admire and love you."

34.4.oldText: Elizabeth's astonishment was beyond words. She stared, blushed, hesitated, and was silent. He took this as sufficient encouragement, and a full confession of everything he felt and had long felt for her immediately followed. He spoke well, but there were feelings besides those of the heart to be expressed, and he was no more eloquent on the subject of love than of pride. His sense of her inferiority, of it being beneath him, of the family obstacles that his judgment had always raised against his inclination—all were dwelt on with a passion that seemed appropriate to the dignity he was sacrificing, but was hardly likely to win her over.

34.6.oldText: "In cases like this, I believe the accepted thing is to express a sense of gratitude for the feelings declared, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that gratitude should be felt, and if I _could_ feel grateful, I would now thank you. But I cannot—I have never wanted your good opinion, and you have certainly given it most reluctantly. I am sorry to have caused anyone pain. It was done entirely without my knowledge, however, and I hope it will be short-lived. The feelings that you say have long prevented you from acknowledging your regard should have little difficulty overcoming it after this explanation."

34.15.oldText: Elizabeth refused to dignify this self-serving remark with a response, but its meaning did not escape her, nor was it likely to soften her feelings.

34.21.oldText: "And this," cried Darcy, pacing quickly across the room, "is your opinion of me! This is how you regard me! I thank you for explaining it so fully. My faults, by this accounting, are heavy indeed! But perhaps," he added, stopping and turning toward her, "these offenses might have been overlooked, had your pride not been hurt by my honest confession of the doubts that had long prevented me from forming any serious intention. These bitter accusations might have been suppressed, had I been more calculating and concealed my inner struggles, and flattered you into believing that I was driven by pure, uncomplicated love—by reason, by reflection, by everything. But dishonesty of every kind is hateful to me. Nor am I ashamed of the feelings I described. They were natural and just. Could you expect me to celebrate the inferiority of your connections? To congratulate myself on the hope of relatives whose position in life is so clearly beneath my own?"

34.27.oldText: "From the very beginning—from the first moment, I may almost say, of my acquaintance with you—your manners, impressing me with the fullest belief in your arrogance, your conceit, and your selfish contempt for the feelings of others, laid the groundwork of a disapproval on which subsequent events have built such an unshakeable dislike that I had not known you a month before I felt you were the last man in the world I could ever be persuaded to marry."

34.29.oldText: And with these words he quickly left the room, and Elizabeth heard him the next moment open the front door and leave the house. The turmoil in her mind was now painfully intense. She did not know how to support herself, and from actual weakness, sat down and cried for half an hour. Her astonishment, as she reflected on what had happened, grew with every review of it. That she should receive a proposal from Mr. Darcy! That he should have been in love with her for so many months! So much in love as to wish to marry her despite all the objections that had made him prevent his friend from marrying her sister, and that must seem at least equally powerful in his own case—it was almost unbelievable! It was gratifying to have unconsciously inspired such a strong attachment. But his pride, his hateful pride, his shameless admission of what he had done to Jane, his unforgivable confidence in confessing what he could not justify, and the callous manner in which he had spoken of Mr. Wickham—whose cruel treatment he had not even tried to deny—soon overwhelmed the pity that the thought of his love had briefly stirred.

35.1.oldText: After walking two or three times along that stretch of lane, she was tempted by the pleasant morning to stop at the gates and look into the park. The five weeks she had now spent in Kent had made a great difference to the landscape, and every day was adding to the greenness of the early trees. She was about to continue her walk when she caught a glimpse of a gentleman within the grove that bordered the park. He was moving her way, and fearing it might be Mr. Darcy, she turned to retreat at once. But the approaching figure was now close enough to see her, and stepping forward eagerly, called her name. She had turned away, but hearing herself called—though in a voice she recognized as Mr. Darcy's—she moved back toward the gate. He had reached it at the same time and, holding out a letter, which she instinctively took, said with a look of proud composure, "I have been walking in the grove for some time, hoping to meet you. Will you do me the honor of reading this letter?" And then, with a slight bow, he turned back into the trees and was soon out of sight.

35.3.oldText: "Do not be alarmed, madam, on receiving this letter, by any fear that it contains a repetition of the feelings, or a renewal of the offers, that were so repugnant to you last night. I write with no intention of causing you pain, or humbling myself, by dwelling on wishes that, for both our sakes, cannot be forgotten soon enough. The effort involved in writing and reading this letter should have been spared, had my honor not required it to be written and read. You must therefore forgive the liberty I take in asking for your attention; your feelings, I know, will give it reluctantly, but I ask it in the name of fairness.

35.4.oldText: "Two offenses of a very different nature, and by no means equal in seriousness, you charged me with last night. The first was that, without regard for the feelings of either party, I had separated Mr. Bingley from your sister. The second was that I had, in defiance of every claim and in defiance of honor and decency, ruined the present welfare and future prospects of Mr. Wickham. To have deliberately and cruelly cast off the companion of my youth, the acknowledged favorite of my father, a young man with scarcely any other support than our patronage, and who had been raised to expect it, would be a wickedness to which the separation of two young people whose attachment had developed over only a few weeks could bear no comparison. But I hope to be cleared hereafter of the severity of the blame so freely given last night, once the following account of my actions and their motives has been read. If, in the explanation that I owe to myself, I am forced to relate feelings that may offend yours, I can only say I am sorry. The necessity must be obeyed, and further apology would be absurd. I had not been long in Hertfordshire before I saw, along with others, that Bingley preferred your elder sister to every other young woman in the area. But it was not until the evening of the dance at Netherfield that I had any concern about a serious attachment. I had often seen him in love before. At that ball, while I had the honor of dancing with you, I first learned from Sir William Lucas's casual remark that Bingley's attentions to your sister had given rise to a general expectation of their marriage. He spoke of it as a certainty, with only the timing undecided. From that moment I watched my friend's behavior carefully, and I could see that his preference for Miss Bennet went beyond anything I had ever witnessed in him. Your sister I watched too. Her look and manners were open, cheerful, and engaging as ever, but without any sign of special feeling in return. And I remained convinced, from that evening's observation, that though she received his attentions with pleasure, she did not invite them by returning the sentiment. If _you_ have not been mistaken about this, _I_ must have been wrong. Your greater knowledge of your sister makes the latter more likely. If it is so—if I was misled by this error into causing her pain—then your resentment has not been unreasonable. But I will not hesitate to say that the composure of your sister's face and manner was such as might have convinced the sharpest observer that, however sweet her temperament, her heart was not likely to be easily touched. That I _wanted_ to believe her indifferent is certain, but I venture to say that my judgments are not usually swayed by my hopes or fears. I did not believe her indifferent because I wished it; I believed it from honest conviction, as truly as I wished it on rational grounds. My objections to the marriage were not merely those I admitted last night—objections that required the strongest passion to overcome in my own case. The lack of important connections could not matter as much to my friend as to me. But there were other reasons for disapproval—reasons that, though they still exist and exist equally in both cases, I had tried to forget because they were not immediately in front of me. These reasons must be stated, though briefly. The position of your mother's family, though not ideal, was nothing compared to the complete lack of propriety so frequently—so almost constantly—displayed by your mother herself, by your three younger sisters, and occasionally even by your father. Forgive me—it pains me to offend you. But amid your own concern for the faults of your closest relatives, and your displeasure at this account of them, let it comfort you to know that you and your eldest sister have conducted yourselves so as to escape any share of this criticism—praise that is as widely given as it is deserved by the good sense and character of you both. I will only add that the events of that evening confirmed my opinion of all parties and strengthened every reason I already had for saving my friend from what I considered a very unhappy match. He left Netherfield for London the next day, as you certainly remember, intending to return soon. My own part must now be explained. His sisters' anxiety had been aroused as much as my own. Our shared feelings were quickly discovered, and recognizing that there was no time to lose in drawing their brother away, we soon decided to follow him directly to London. We went accordingly, and I readily took on the task of pointing out to my friend the certain dangers of such a choice. I described and pressed them seriously. But however much this argument might have shaken or delayed his decision, I do not think it would ultimately have prevented the marriage, had it not been supported by my assurance—which I did not hesitate to give—of your sister's indifference. He had believed she returned his feelings with sincere, if not equal, regard. But Bingley has great natural humility, with a stronger reliance on my judgment than on his own. Convincing him that he had been mistaken was therefore not very difficult. Persuading him not to return to Hertfordshire, once that conviction was established, was hardly the work of a moment. I cannot blame myself for having done this much. There is only one part of my behavior in the whole affair that I do not look back on with satisfaction: that I stooped to being deceptive enough to hide from him the fact that your sister was in London. I knew it myself, as did Miss Bingley, but her brother is still unaware of it. That they might have met without harm is perhaps likely, but his feelings did not seem to me extinguished enough for him to see her without some risk. Perhaps this concealment was beneath me. It is done, however, and it was done for the best. On this subject I have nothing more to say, no other apology to make. If I have hurt your sister's feelings, it was done unknowingly; and though the motives that guided me may naturally seem insufficient to you, I have not yet learned to condemn them. Regarding that other, more serious accusation—of having wronged Mr. Wickham—I can only refute it by laying before you the full history of his connection with my family. I do not know what he has specifically accused me of, but I can summon more than one witness of unquestionable honesty to verify what I shall relate. Mr. Wickham is the son of a very respectable man who for many years managed all the Pemberley estates, and whose faithful service naturally inclined my father to help him. On George Wickham, who was his godson, my father's generosity was therefore freely lavished. My father paid for his schooling and later for Cambridge—crucial support, since Wickham's own father, always poor due to his wife's extravagance, would have been unable to give him a gentleman's education. My father was not only fond of this young man's company—his manners were always charming—he also had the highest opinion of him, and hoping he would enter the clergy, intended to provide for him in it. As for myself, it is many, many years since I first began to see him very differently. The vicious tendencies and lack of principle that he was careful to hide from his best patron could not escape the notice of a young man nearly his own age, who had chances to observe him in unguarded moments that Mr. Darcy never had. Here again I shall cause you pain—to what degree, only you can tell. But whatever feelings Mr. Wickham may have created in you, a suspicion of their nature shall not prevent me from revealing his true character. It only adds another reason to do so. My excellent father died about five years ago, and his attachment to Mr. Wickham was steadfast to the end—in his will he specifically asked me to advance Wickham's career as his profession allowed, and if he entered the clergy, to give him a valuable family parish as soon as it became vacant. There was also a legacy of one thousand pounds. Wickham's own father did not long survive mine, and within six months of these events, Mr. Wickham wrote to tell me that, having finally decided against entering the clergy, he hoped I would not think it unreasonable of him to expect some more immediate financial benefit in place of the parish appointment, from which he could not benefit. He had some intention, he said, of studying law, and I must realize that the interest on one thousand pounds would be very inadequate support for that. I hoped more than believed he was sincere, but was perfectly willing to agree to his proposal. I knew Mr. Wickham should not be a clergyman. The matter was quickly settled. He gave up all claim to help in the church, should he ever be in a position to receive it, and accepted three thousand pounds in return. All connection between us seemed dissolved. I thought too badly of him to invite him to Pemberley or accept his company in London. In London, I believe, he mainly lived, but his study of law was merely a pretense, and being now free from all restraint, his life was one of laziness and excess. For about three years I heard little of him, but when the incumbent of the parish that had been intended for him died, he wrote to me again to request the appointment. His circumstances, he assured me—and I had no difficulty believing it—were extremely bad. He had found law a most unprofitable study and was now absolutely determined to be ordained, if I would grant him the position—which he trusted I could hardly refuse, since he was sure I had no one else to provide for, and could not have forgotten my late father's wishes. You will hardly blame me for refusing this request, or for resisting every repetition of it. His resentment was proportional to his desperation, and he was doubtless as vicious in his abuse of me to others as in his reproaches to me directly. After this period, all pretense of acquaintance was dropped. How he lived, I do not know. But last summer he was again most painfully forced on my attention. I must now mention something I would prefer to forget—something that nothing less than the present obligation would induce me to reveal to anyone. Having said this much, I have no doubt of your discretion. My sister, who is more than ten years younger than I, was left to the joint guardianship of my mother's nephew, Colonel Fitzwilliam, and myself. About a year ago she was taken from school and a household was established for her in London. Last summer she went with the woman who ran her household to Ramsgate, and there Mr. Wickham also went—undoubtedly by design. It turned out there was a prior connection between him and Mrs. Younge, in whose character we were most unfortunately deceived. With her help and encouragement, he so far ingratiated himself with Georgiana—whose loving heart still held a strong memory of his kindness to her as a child—that she was persuaded to believe herself in love and agreed to an elopement. She was only fifteen, which must be her excuse. And after stating her foolishness, I am happy to add that I learned of it from her own confession. I joined them unexpectedly a day or two before the planned elopement, and Georgiana, unable to bear the thought of grieving and offending a brother she almost looked up to as a father, told me everything. You can imagine what I felt and how I acted. Concern for my sister's reputation and feelings prevented any public exposure, but I wrote to Mr. Wickham, who left immediately, and Mrs. Younge was of course dismissed. Mr. Wickham's chief motive was undoubtedly my sister's fortune, which is thirty thousand pounds, but I cannot help thinking that the hope of revenge against me was a strong incentive. His revenge would have been complete indeed. This, madam, is a truthful account of every event that has connected us, and if you do not absolutely reject it as false, I hope you will from now on acquit me of cruelty toward Mr. Wickham. I do not know in what way, or with what falsehoods, he has deceived you, but his success is perhaps not surprising, given how ignorant you were of everything concerning either of us. You could not possibly have detected him, and you certainly were not inclined to suspect him. You may wonder why all this was not told you last night. But I was not enough in command of myself then to know what should or could be revealed. For the truth of everything related here, I can appeal especially to the testimony of Colonel Fitzwilliam, who, from our close family ties and constant friendship—and even more as one of the executors of my father's will—has necessarily been informed of every detail of these matters. If your hatred of _me_ should make _my_ word worthless, you cannot be prevented by the same reason from trusting my cousin. And so that you may have the chance to consult him, I shall try to find an opportunity to put this letter in your hands this morning. I will only add, God bless you.

36.0.oldText: When Mr. Darcy gave Elizabeth the letter, she didn't expect it to contain a renewed proposal—she had formed no expectations at all about its contents. But whatever they might be, it's easy to imagine how eagerly she read through them, and what a turmoil of conflicting emotions they stirred up. Her feelings as she read could hardly be described. She was astonished to discover that he believed he had any apology to make, and she was firmly convinced that he could offer no explanation that wouldn't be better concealed out of decent shame. With a strong prejudice against everything he might say, she began reading his account of what had happened at Netherfield. She read with an eagerness that hardly left her the ability to understand, and in her impatience to know what the next sentence would bring, she couldn't take in the meaning of the one before her eyes. She instantly decided his claim about her sister's indifference must be false, and his account of the real—the worst—objections to the match made her too angry to want to be fair to him. The regret he expressed for what he'd done didn't satisfy her; his tone wasn't apologetic but arrogant. It was all pride and insolence.

36.2.oldText: In this agitated state of mind, with thoughts that couldn't settle on anything, she walked on; but it was no use—within half a minute the letter was unfolded again, and pulling herself together as best she could, she began the humiliating task of rereading everything about Wickham, forcing herself to examine the meaning of every sentence. The account of his connection with the Pemberley family was exactly what he himself had told her, and the kindness of the late Mr. Darcy, though she hadn't previously known its full extent, matched his own words equally well. So far each account confirmed the other; but when she came to the will, the difference was enormous. What Wickham had said about the living was fresh in her memory, and as she recalled his very words, it was impossible not to feel that there was gross dishonesty on one side or the other; for a few moments she flattered herself that her own judgment wasn't wrong. But when she read and reread, with the closest attention, the details of Wickham's giving up all claim to the living, and his receiving instead the considerable sum of three thousand pounds, she was forced to hesitate again. She put down the letter, weighed every circumstance with what she intended to be impartiality—considered the likelihood of each claim—but with little success. On both sides it was only assertion. Again she read on. But every line proved more clearly that the affair, which she had believed impossible to misrepresent in any way that could make Mr. Darcy's conduct less than disgraceful, was capable of an interpretation that made him entirely blameless throughout the whole matter.

36.3.oldText: The extravagance and general misconduct he didn't hesitate to lay at Mr. Wickham's door shocked her deeply—all the more because she could produce no evidence against the charges. She had never heard of him before he joined the ——shire militia, which he'd entered at the urging of the young man who, meeting him by chance in London, had renewed a slight acquaintance. Of his previous way of life, nothing had been known in Hertfordshire except what he'd told

36.4.oldText: them himself. As to his real character, even if she'd had the means to investigate, she had never felt the slightest urge to do so. His face, his voice, and his manner had immediately established him in possession of every virtue. She tried to recall some example of goodness, some distinguished mark of integrity or kindness, that might rescue him from Mr. Darcy's accusations; or at least, through the weight of virtue, make up for those minor failings she would try to classify Mr. Darcy's description of years of idleness and vice as being. But no such memory came to her aid. She could see him instantly before her, with all the charm of his bearing and address, but she could remember nothing more substantial than the general approval of the neighborhood and the regard his social skills had earned him in the officers' mess. After pausing on this point for a considerable while, she continued reading once more. But the story that followed, of his designs on Miss Darcy, was confirmed to some extent by what had passed between Colonel Fitzwilliam and herself only the morning before; and she was finally directed to Colonel Fitzwilliam himself for the truth of every detail—the very man from whom she had already heard of his close involvement in all his cousin's affairs, and whose character she had no reason to question. At one point she had almost decided to ask him directly, but the awkwardness of such a request held her back, and the idea was finally banished altogether by the certainty that Mr. Darcy would never have risked such a claim if he hadn't been sure of his cousin's confirmation.

36.5.oldText: She remembered perfectly everything that had passed between Wickham and herself in their first evening at Mr. Philips's. Many of his exact words were still fresh in her memory. She was now struck by the impropriety of such disclosures to a stranger, and wondered how it had escaped her notice before. She saw the indelicacy of putting himself forward as he had done, and the inconsistency between what he professed and how he actually behaved. She remembered that he had boasted of having no fear of seeing Mr. Darcy—that Mr. Darcy might leave the country, but he would stand his ground; yet he had avoided the Netherfield ball the very next week. She also remembered that until the Netherfield family had left the area, he had told his story to no one but herself; but after their departure, it had been discussed everywhere; that he'd then had no restraint, no scruples about destroying Mr. Darcy's reputation, though he had assured her that respect for the father would always prevent him from exposing the son.

36.6.oldText: How differently everything now appeared where he was concerned! His attentions to Miss King were now clearly the result of purely mercenary motives, and the modesty of her fortune proved not the moderation of his desires but his eagerness to grab at anything. His behavior toward Elizabeth herself could now have had no decent motive: he had either been mistaken about her fortune, or had been flattering his vanity by encouraging the preference she believed she had shown all too clearly. Every lingering impulse to defend him grew fainter and fainter; and in further justification of Mr. Darcy, she had to admit that Mr. Bingley, when questioned by Jane, had long ago confirmed his blamelessness in the affair—that, proud and off-putting as his manners were, she had never, in the whole course of their acquaintance (an acquaintance which had lately brought them together often, giving her a sort of familiarity with his ways) seen anything that betrayed him as unprincipled or unjust—anything that suggested irreligious or immoral habits—that among his own circle he was respected and valued—that even Wickham had granted him credit as a brother, and she had often heard him speak so affectionately of his sister as to prove him capable of genuine feeling—that had his actions been what Wickham claimed, such a gross violation of everything right could hardly have been hidden from the world; and that friendship between a man capable of such things and someone as decent as Mr. Bingley was simply impossible to explain.

36.7.oldText: She grew absolutely ashamed of herself. She couldn't think of either Darcy or Wickham without feeling that she had been blind, biased, prejudiced, and absurd.

36.8.oldText: "How shamefully I've behaved!" she cried. "I, who prided myself on my judgment! I, who valued myself on my abilities! who often scorned the generous openness of my sister, and satisfied my vanity with useless or pointless suspicion. How humiliating this discovery is! And yet, how deserved the humiliation! If I had been in love, I couldn't have been more wretchedly blind. But vanity, not love, has been my downfall. Pleased by one man's preference and offended by the other's neglect, right from the very start of our acquaintance, I courted bias and ignorance, and pushed reason aside wherever either of them was concerned. Until this moment, I never truly knew myself."

36.9.oldText: From herself to Jane, from Jane to Bingley, her thoughts followed a line which soon reminded her that Mr. Darcy's explanation on that score had seemed very inadequate; and she read it again. The effect of a second reading was entirely different. How could she deny credit to his claims in one case when she had been forced to accept them in the other? He declared himself to have been completely unaware of her sister's feelings, and she couldn't help remembering that Charlotte's opinion had always been the same. Nor could she deny the accuracy of his description of Jane. She felt that Jane's feelings, though deep, were rarely displayed, and that there was a habitual composure in her manner not often combined with great depth of feeling.

36.10.oldText: When she came to the part of the letter where her family was mentioned, in tones of such mortifying yet deserved criticism, her sense of shame was intense. The justice of the charge struck her too powerfully to deny; and the specific incidents he referred to at the Netherfield ball, which confirmed all his initial disapproval, couldn't have made a stronger impression on his mind than they now made on hers.

36.11.oldText: The compliment to herself and her sister was not unappreciated. It was soothing, but it couldn't console her for the contempt their behavior had brought upon the rest of her family; and as she considered that Jane's disappointment had, in fact, been the work of their closest relations, and reflected how seriously the reputation of both sisters must be damaged by such improper conduct, she felt more depressed than she had ever known.

36.12.oldText: After wandering along the lane for two hours, giving way to every kind of thought—reconsidering events, weighing probabilities, and reconciling herself as well as she could to a change so sudden and so significant—fatigue and the realization of her long absence finally made her turn for home. She entered the house determined to appear as cheerful as usual, and resolved to suppress the kind of reflections that would make her unfit for conversation.

36.13.oldText: She was immediately told that the two gentlemen from Rosings had each called during her absence; Mr. Darcy only for a few minutes, to say goodbye, but Colonel Fitzwilliam had been sitting with them for at least an hour, hoping she would return, and had nearly decided to go looking for her. Elizabeth could only pretend to be sorry she'd missed him; she was actually relieved. Colonel Fitzwilliam was no longer of any interest to her. She could think of nothing but the letter.

37.3.oldText: Mr. Collins had a compliment and a subtle reference to offer here, which were kindly smiled upon by both mother and daughter.

37.9.oldText: "Oh, your father can certainly spare you if your mother can. Daughters are never of much importance to a father. And if you'll stay another full month, I'll be able to take one of you as far as London, since I'm going there in early June for a week. And since Dawson doesn't mind riding on top, there will be plenty of room for one of you—and if the weather happens to be cool, I wouldn't object to taking you both, since neither of you is particularly large."

37.11.oldText: Lady Catherine seemed resigned. "Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always speak my mind, and I can't bear the idea of two young women traveling by post alone. It's highly improper. You must arrange to send somebody. I have the strongest objection to that sort of thing. Young women should always be properly guarded and accompanied, according to their station in life. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I insisted she have two men-servants with her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley and Lady Anne, couldn't properly have appeared in any other style. I'm extremely attentive to all these things. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I'm glad I thought to mention it; for it would really be a discredit to you to let them go alone."

37.16.oldText: Worry about Jane was another persistent concern; and Mr. Darcy's explanation, by restoring Bingley to all her former good opinion, sharpened the sense of what Jane had lost. His affection had been proven sincere, and his conduct cleared of all blame, unless some could be attached to his too-implicit trust in his friend. How painful then was the thought that Jane had been denied a situation so desirable in every way, so full of advantage, so promising of happiness—all because of the foolishness and impropriety of her own family!

38.2.oldText: Elizabeth was eager with her thanks and assurances of happiness. She had spent six weeks with great enjoyment, and the pleasure of being with Charlotte, and the kind attention she had received, must make her feel the grateful one. Mr. Collins was gratified, and with a more smiling solemnity replied—

38.6.oldText: Elizabeth could safely say that it was a great happiness when that was the case, and with equal sincerity could add that she truly believed in and was glad of his domestic comforts. She wasn't sorry, however, to have the recital interrupted by the entrance of the lady who was its subject. Poor Charlotte! It was sad to leave her to such company! But she had chosen it with her eyes open; and though she clearly regretted that her visitors were leaving, she didn't seem to be asking for pity. Her home and her housekeeping, her parish and her poultry, and all related concerns had not yet lost their charm.

38.16.oldText: It took some effort, meanwhile, for her to wait even for Longbourn before telling her sister about Mr. Darcy's proposal. To know that she had the power to reveal something that would utterly astonish Jane, and must at the same time gratify whatever of her own vanity she hadn't yet managed to reason away, was such a temptation to openness that nothing could have overcome it—except her uncertainty about how much she should share, and her fear that if she once began, she might be drawn into repeating something about Bingley that would only cause her sister further pain.

39.0.oldText: It was the second week of May when the three young ladies set out together from Gracechurch Street for the town of —— in Hertfordshire; and as they drew near the inn where Mr. Bennet's carriage was to meet them, they quickly spotted both Kitty and Lydia looking out from a dining room upstairs. These two girls had been there for over an hour, happily occupied in browsing the milliner's shop across the street, watching the soldier on guard duty, and preparing a salad.

39.13.oldText: "I'm sure there isn't on his. I'll answer for it—he never cared a bit about her. Who could, about such a plain little freckled thing?"

39.14.oldText: Elizabeth was shocked to realize that, however incapable she herself was of such crude language, the crudeness of the sentiment was hardly different from what she had once felt and considered perfectly reasonable!

39.18.oldText: Their reception at home was most kind. Mrs. Bennet was delighted to see Jane looking as beautiful as ever; and more than once during dinner Mr. Bennet said voluntarily to Elizabeth—

39.21.oldText: "Oh, Mary," she said, "I wish you'd come with us, because we had such fun! As we went along, Kitty and I pulled up all the carriage blinds and pretended no one was inside; and I would have kept it up the whole way if Kitty hadn't gotten carsick. And when we reached the George, I think we behaved beautifully, because we treated the other three to the nicest cold lunch in the world, and if you'd been there, we would have treated you too. And then when we left, it was such fun! I thought we'd never get into the carriage. I was ready to die of laughing. And then we were so merry all the way home! We talked and laughed so loud that anyone could have heard us for miles!"

39.24.oldText: That afternoon Lydia was insistent that the rest of the girls walk to Meryton to see how everyone was doing; but Elizabeth firmly opposed the idea. It shouldn't be said that the Miss Bennets couldn't be at home half a day before they were chasing after the officers. There was another reason too for her opposition. She dreaded seeing Wickham again and was determined to avoid it as long as possible. The comfort of the regiment's approaching departure was truly beyond words. In two weeks they would be gone, and once they were, she hoped there would be nothing more to trouble her on his account.

40.5.oldText: "But you blame me for speaking so harshly about Wickham?"

40.18.oldText: "Indeed I couldn't. I was uncomfortable enough—I was very uncomfortable—I might say unhappy. And with no one to talk to about what I felt, no Jane to comfort me and tell me I hadn't been quite so vain and foolish and absurd as I knew I had! Oh, how I needed you!"

40.34.oldText: "No, it would have been strange if they had. But I have no doubt they often discuss it between themselves. Well, if they can feel easy about an estate that isn't rightfully theirs, so much the better. I should be ashamed of having one that was only entailed on me."

41.13.oldText: Elizabeth tried in vain to make her see reason, and Jane to make her accept it. As for Elizabeth herself, this invitation was so far from exciting the same feelings as it did in her mother and Lydia that she saw it as the death sentence for any hope of common sense in Lydia; and as deplorable as such a step would make her look, she couldn't help privately advising her father not to let her go. She laid out for him all the problems with Lydia's general behavior, the little benefit she could get from the friendship of a woman like Mrs. Forster, and the likelihood of her becoming even more reckless with such a companion in Brighton, where the temptations would be far greater than at home. He heard her carefully, and then said—

41.15.oldText: "If you understood," said Elizabeth, "the very serious harm to us all that must come from Lydia's reckless and imprudent behavior—harm which, in fact, has already come from it—I'm sure you would judge the matter differently."

41.21.oldText: Had Lydia and her mother known what Elizabeth had discussed with her father, their outrage would have been hard to contain. In Lydia's imagination, a trip to Brighton encompassed every possible form of earthly happiness. She saw, with the creative eye of fantasy, the streets of that fashionable seaside town filled with officers. She saw herself the center of attention for dozens of them, all currently unknown to her. She saw all the splendors of the camp: its tents stretched out in beautiful uniform rows, crowded with the young and the lively, and dazzling in scarlet; and to complete the picture, she saw herself sitting beneath a tent, tenderly flirting with at least six officers at once.

41.24.oldText: Elizabeth was now to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Having been frequently in his company since her return, her earlier agitation was mostly gone; the excitement of her former partiality had vanished entirely. She had even learned to detect, in the very charm that had first delighted her, an affectation and a sameness that now bored and repelled her. In his current behavior toward her, moreover, she found a fresh source of irritation; for his obvious intention to revive the attention he'd shown early in their acquaintance could only serve, after what she now knew, to annoy her. She lost all concern for him when she found herself singled out for such idle and shallow flirtation; and while she firmly discouraged it, she couldn't help feeling the insult contained in his assumption that, however long and for whatever reason his attentions had been withdrawn, her vanity would be gratified and her preference secured by their mere renewal.

41.25.oldText: On the very last day of the regiment's stay in Meryton, he dined with other officers at Longbourn; and Elizabeth was so little disposed to part from him on good terms that she mentioned Colonel Fitzwilliam's and Mr. Darcy's having both spent three weeks at Rosings, and asked whether he knew the former.

42.0.oldText: Had Elizabeth's views been drawn entirely from her own family, she could not have formed a very flattering picture of married happiness or domestic comfort. Her father, captivated by youth and beauty and that appearance of good humor which youth and beauty generally give, had married a woman whose weak understanding and narrow mind had very early put an end to any real affection for her. Respect, esteem, and trust had vanished forever, and all his visions of domestic happiness had collapsed. But Mr. Bennet was not the sort of man to seek comfort for his own poor judgment in the pleasures that too often console the unfortunate for their foolishness or vice. He was fond of the countryside and of books, and from these interests came his chief enjoyments. To his wife he was hardly indebted at all, except that her ignorance and foolishness had contributed to his amusement. This is not the sort of happiness a man would generally wish to owe to his wife; but where other forms of entertainment are lacking, the true philosopher will make the best of what's available.

42.1.oldText: Elizabeth, however, had never been blind to the problems in her father's behavior as a husband. She had always seen it with pain; but respecting his abilities, and grateful for his affectionate treatment of herself, she had tried to forget what she couldn't overlook, and to push from her thoughts the constant breach of marital duty and decency which, by exposing his wife to the contempt of her own children, was so deeply wrong. But she had never felt as strongly as now the disadvantages facing the children of such an unsuitable marriage, nor been so fully aware of the harm arising from such a misguided use of talent—talent which, properly applied, might at least have preserved the respectability of his daughters, even if it couldn't have broadened his wife's mind.

42.14.oldText: Mrs. Gardiner dismissed her excuse. "If it were merely a fine house with expensive furnishings," she said, "I wouldn't care about it either; but the grounds are delightful. They have some of the finest woods in the country."

43.53.oldText: The others then joined her and expressed their admiration of his appearance; but Elizabeth heard not a word, and entirely absorbed in her own feelings, followed them in silence. She was overwhelmed by shame and embarrassment. Coming here had been the most unfortunate, the most ill-judged thing in the world! How strange it must look to him! In what an unflattering light it might strike so proud a man! It might seem as if she had purposely thrown herself in his path again! Oh, why had she come? Or why had he arrived a day early? Had they been only ten minutes sooner, they would have been beyond his reach; for it was clear he had just that moment arrived, just that moment dismounted from his horse or stepped out of his carriage.
