She blushed again and again at the perversity of this meeting. And his behavior, so strikingly changed—what could it mean? That he should even speak to her was astonishing!—but to speak with such courtesy, to ask about her family! Never in her life had she seen his manners so little dignified, never had he spoken with such gentleness as at this unexpected encounter. What a contrast to his last speech in Rosings Park, when he put his letter into her hand! She didn't know what to think or how to account for it.

43.57.oldText: Mrs. Gardiner was standing a little behind, and when Elizabeth paused, he asked if she would do him the honor of introducing him to her friends. This was a courtesy she was entirely unprepared for; and she could hardly suppress a smile at his now seeking the acquaintance of the very people whose existence his pride had rejected when he proposed to her. "What will his surprise be," she thought, "when he finds out who they are! He takes them for fashionable people."

43.58.oldText: The introduction, however, was made at once; and as she named their relationship to herself, she stole a glance at him to see how he took it, half expecting him to flee from such embarrassing connections. That he was surprised was obvious; but he bore it well, and far from retreating, turned back with them and struck up a conversation with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth couldn't help being pleased—couldn't help feeling a small triumph. It was comforting to know she had some relatives who would not cause embarrassment. She listened carefully to everything they said and took pride in every remark of her uncle's that showed his intelligence, his good taste, or his fine manners.

43.60.oldText: After walking some time in this way—the two ladies in front, the two gentlemen behind—they changed positions when they went down to the riverbank to examine some unusual water plant. The rearrangement was Mrs. Gardiner's doing: tired from the morning's exercise, she found Elizabeth's arm an inadequate support and preferred her husband's. Mr. Darcy took her place beside Elizabeth, and they walked on together. After a brief silence, Elizabeth spoke first. She wanted him to know she had been told he was away before she came, and so she began by saying that his arrival had been very unexpected—"because your housekeeper told us you definitely wouldn't be here until tomorrow, and before we left Bakewell, we understood you weren't expected in the area at all." He confirmed this was true, and said that business with his steward had brought him ahead of the rest of his party. "They'll join me early tomorrow," he continued, "and among them are some people you know—Mr. Bingley and his sisters."

43.64.oldText: They now walked on in silence, each deep in thought. Elizabeth was not comfortable—that was impossible—but she was flattered and pleased. His wish to introduce his sister was a compliment of the highest order. They soon outpaced the others, and when they reached the carriage, Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner were still a good distance behind.

43.73.oldText: "But he may just be putting on a show of civility," replied her uncle. "Important men often do that. So I won't take him at his word about the fishing, since he might change his mind and throw me off his property."

44.0.oldText: Elizabeth had assumed that Mr. Darcy would bring his sister to visit her the day after she arrived at Pemberley, and had therefore resolved not to leave the inn the whole morning. But she was wrong; for on the very morning after their own arrival at Lambton, the visitors came. They had been walking around the town with some of their new friends and had just returned to the inn to change for dinner with the same family, when the sound of a carriage drew them to the window, and they saw a gentleman and lady in a light open carriage driving up the street. Elizabeth immediately recognized the livery, guessed what it meant, and surprised her relatives considerably by telling them about the honor she expected. Her uncle and aunt were all amazement; and the embarrassment of her manner, combined with the visit itself and many details from the day before, opened up a new possibility in their minds. Nothing had ever suggested it before, but they now felt there was no other way to explain such attention from such a source than by supposing he was attracted to their niece. While these newly formed ideas were forming in their heads, Elizabeth's agitation was growing by the moment. She was amazed at her own nervousness; but among other causes for unease, she worried that the brother might have said too much in her favor, and more than usually anxious to make a good impression, she naturally feared she would fail completely.

44.7.oldText: In watching Bingley, her thoughts naturally flew to her sister; and oh, how intensely she longed to know whether any of his thoughts were similarly directed. Sometimes she fancied he talked less than on previous occasions, and once or twice imagined that, as he looked at her, he was trying to trace a resemblance. But though this might be imaginary, she could not be mistaken about his behavior toward Miss Darcy, who had been set up as Jane's rival. There was nothing on either side to suggest particular affection. Nothing passed between them that could justify his sister's hopes. On this point she was soon reassured; and two or three small incidents before they parted, which in her anxious interpretation suggested memories of Jane—not untouched by tenderness—and a wish to say more that might lead to mentioning her, had he dared. He remarked to her, in a quiet moment when the others were talking, with something of real regret in his tone, that "it had been a very long time since he'd had the pleasure of seeing her." And before she could reply, he added, "It's been over eight months. We haven't met since November 26th, when we were all dancing together at Netherfield."

44.9.oldText: She seldom turned her eyes toward Mr. Darcy himself; but whenever she did steal a glance, she saw an expression of general warmth, and in everything he said she heard a tone so completely free of the arrogance or disdain of his companions that she was convinced the improved manners she had seen yesterday—however temporary they might prove—had at least lasted more than one day. When she saw him actively seeking the acquaintance and courting the good opinion of people whose company, only a few months ago, he would have considered beneath him; when she saw him so civil not only to herself but to the very relatives he had openly looked down upon, and when she remembered their last lively scene at Hunsford Parsonage—the difference, the change, was so great that it struck her forcibly, and she could hardly keep her astonishment from showing. Never, even among his close friends at Netherfield or his grand relatives at Rosings, had she seen him so eager to please, so free from self-importance or stiffness, as now—when nothing could be gained from the effort, and when the very acquaintance of those he was being attentive to would be mocked by the ladies of both Netherfield and Rosings.

44.10.oldText: Their visitors stayed for over half an hour, and when they rose to leave, Mr. Darcy asked his sister to join him in inviting Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner and Miss Bennet to dinner at Pemberley before they left the area. Miss Darcy, though with a shyness that showed she wasn't used to giving invitations, readily agreed. Mrs. Gardiner looked at her niece, wanting to know how she—the one the invitation most concerned—felt about accepting, but Elizabeth had turned away. Assuming, however, that this deliberate avoidance came from momentary embarrassment rather than actual reluctance, and seeing in her husband—who was fond of company—a perfect willingness to accept, she ventured to say yes for all of them, and the day after next was fixed.

44.13.oldText: As for Mr. Darcy, it was now a matter of some importance to Elizabeth to think well of him; and as far as their acquaintance went, there was nothing to criticize. They couldn't help being struck by his politeness, and had they judged his character from their own experience and his servant's report alone, ignoring all other accounts, nobody in Hertfordshire would have recognized the description. There was now a reason to believe the housekeeper, and they soon came to feel that the authority of a servant who had known him since he was four years old, and whose own manners showed respectability, was not to be lightly dismissed. Nor had anything they heard from their Lambton friends undermined it. The only charge against him was pride; and he probably did have pride—if not, it would certainly be attributed to him by the inhabitants of a small market town where the family didn't mix socially. It was acknowledged, however, that he was a generous man who did much good among the poor.

44.15.oldText: As for Elizabeth, her thoughts were at Pemberley that evening even more than the night before; and the evening, though it seemed long as it passed, was not long enough to sort out her feelings about one particular person in that house. She lay awake for two full hours trying to understand them. She certainly didn't hate him. No—hatred had vanished long ago, and she had been almost as long ashamed of ever having felt a dislike strong enough to deserve that name. The respect born from recognizing his genuine qualities, though initially resisted, had for some time ceased to be unwelcome; and it was now heightened into something friendlier by the testimony so strongly in his favor, casting his character in such a good light, that yesterday had produced. But above all—above respect and esteem—there was a feeling of goodwill that couldn't be ignored. It was gratitude: gratitude not merely for having once loved her, but for loving her still enough to forgive all the rudeness and bitterness of her manner in rejecting him, and all the unfair accusations that had accompanied her rejection. He, whom she had been certain would avoid her as his greatest enemy, seemed—at this accidental meeting—most eager to continue their acquaintance. And without any showy display of affection, or any special manner when the two of them were alone, he was seeking the good opinion of her friends and determined to introduce her to his sister. Such a change in a man of so much pride stirred not only astonishment but gratitude—for it could only be explained by deep, genuine love; and as such, its effect on her was of a kind to be encouraged, by no means unpleasant, though she couldn't quite define it. She respected him, she esteemed him, she was grateful to him, she felt a real interest in his wellbeing; and she only wanted to know how far she wished that wellbeing to depend on herself, and how far it would be for the happiness of both if she were to use the power—which she had a feeling she still possessed—to encourage him to propose again.

45.0.oldText: Convinced as Elizabeth now was that Miss Bingley's dislike of her had originated in jealousy, she couldn't help wondering how coldly or civilly that lady would treat her now.

45.7.oldText: He had been with Mr. Gardiner and two or three other gentlemen by the river, and had only left them on learning that the ladies of the family planned to visit Georgiana that morning. No sooner did he appear than Elizabeth wisely resolved to be perfectly relaxed and natural—a resolution all the more necessary because she could see that every eye in the room was watching his behavior. In no face was eager curiosity more plainly visible than in Miss Bingley's, despite the smiles she put on whenever she spoke to either Darcy or his sister; for jealousy had not yet made her desperate, and her pursuit of Mr. Darcy was far from over. Miss Darcy, on her brother's entrance, made a much greater effort to join the conversation; and Elizabeth saw that he was anxious for his sister and herself to become friends, and encouraged every attempt at conversation on either side. Miss Bingley saw all this too; and in the recklessness of anger, she seized the first chance to say, with sneering politeness—

45.9.oldText: In Darcy's presence she didn't dare say Wickham's name; but Elizabeth instantly understood who she was referring to, and the various memories connected with him caused a moment's pain. But gathering herself to repel the mean-spirited attack, she answered the question in a reasonably composed tone. While she spoke, an involuntary glance showed her Darcy with a heightened color, looking at her intently, and his sister overcome with confusion, unable to raise her eyes. Had Miss Bingley known what pain she was causing her beloved friend, she would certainly have held back; but she had only meant to embarrass Elizabeth by bringing up a man she believed Elizabeth was attracted to, hoping to make her betray a sensitivity that might damage her in Darcy's eyes—and perhaps remind him of all the foolishness by which some of her family were connected to that regiment. Not a whisper had ever reached her of Miss Darcy's near-elopement. It had been kept secret from everyone possible, except Elizabeth; and from all of Bingley's connections, Darcy was particularly anxious to conceal it, because of his very hope that those connections might one day become his own. He had certainly formed such a plan; and though he didn't intend it to influence his efforts to separate Bingley from Miss Bennet, it probably added to his concern for his friend's welfare.

45.14.oldText: "For my own part," she continued, "I must say I never could see any beauty in her. Her face is too thin; her complexion has no glow; and her features are not at all handsome. Her nose has no character; there's nothing distinctive about it. Her teeth are acceptable but nothing special; and as for her eyes, which have sometimes been called fine, I never could see anything extraordinary about them. They have a sharp, shrewd look that I don't like at all; and in her whole bearing there's a self-assurance without elegance that's intolerable."

46.0.oldText: Elizabeth had been quite disappointed not to find a letter from Jane when they first arrived at Lambton; and this disappointment had been renewed each morning since. But on the third day her patience was rewarded by the arrival of two letters at once, one of which was marked as having been misdirected. Elizabeth wasn't surprised, since Jane had addressed it remarkably badly.

46.2.oldText: "Since writing the above, dearest Lizzy, something has happened of a most unexpected and serious nature; but I'm afraid of alarming you—rest assured that we are all well. What I have to say concerns poor Lydia. An express messenger came at midnight, just as we had all gone to bed, from Colonel Forster, to inform us that she had run off to Scotland with one of his officers; to tell the truth, with Wickham! Imagine our surprise. To Kitty, however, it doesn't seem entirely unexpected. I am very, very sorry. Such an imprudent match on both sides! But I'm willing to hope for the best, and that his character has been misunderstood. I can easily believe him thoughtless and irresponsible, but this step (and let us take comfort from it) suggests nothing truly wicked at heart. His choice is at least disinterested, since he must know my father can give her nothing. Our poor mother is dreadfully upset. My father is handling it better. How grateful I am that we never told them what had been said against him; we must forget it ourselves. They left Saturday night around midnight, as far as anyone can tell, but weren't missed until yesterday morning at eight. The express was sent immediately. My dear Lizzy, they must have passed within ten miles of us. Colonel Forster expects to be here soon. Lydia left a few lines for his wife, telling her what they intended. I must stop, because I can't be away from our poor mother for long. I'm afraid you won't be able to make out what I've written, but I hardly know what I'm saying."

46.4.oldText: "By now, my dearest sister, you've received my hurried letter; I hope this one will be more coherent, but though I'm not rushed for time, my head is so confused that I can't promise to make sense. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what to write, but I have bad news that can't be delayed. Imprudent as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we now desperately hope it has taken place, because there's too much reason to fear they haven't gone to Scotland after all. Colonel Forster came yesterday, having left Brighton the day before, just hours after the express. Though Lydia's short note to Mrs. Forster said they were going to Gretna Green, something Denny let slip suggested he believed Wickham never meant to go there, or to marry Lydia at all. This was reported to Colonel Forster, who immediately set out from Brighton to trace their route. He tracked them easily to Clapham, but no farther; for there they switched from their hired carriage to a hackney coach and sent the first one back to Epsom. All that's known after that is they were seen continuing toward London. I don't know what to think. After making every possible inquiry in that part of London, Colonel Forster came on to Hertfordshire, checking at every turnpike and inn along the way, but with no success—nobody matching their description had been seen. With the kindest concern, he came to Longbourn and broke his fears to us in the most tactful way possible. I feel deeply sorry for him and Mrs. Forster, but no one can blame them. Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is very great. My father and mother believe the worst, but I can't think so badly of him. There are many reasons it might have been more practical for them to marry privately in London rather than follow their original plan; and even if he could form such a design against a girl from Lydia's family—which is surely unlikely—can I believe she's so lost to everything? Impossible! I'm sorry to find, however, that Colonel Forster doesn't expect them to have married; he shook his head when I expressed my hopes, and said he feared Wickham was not a man to be trusted. My poor mother is really ill and keeps to her room. Could she exert herself, it would be better, but that's not to be expected; and as for my father, I never in my life saw him so affected. Poor Kitty is furious at having been sworn to secrecy about their attachment, but since it was told in confidence, one can't blame her. I'm truly glad, dearest Lizzy, that you've been spared these awful scenes; but now that the first shock is over, shall I admit that I long for your return? I'm not so selfish as to press for it if it's inconvenient. Goodbye! I pick up my pen again to do what I just said I wouldn't; but the situation is such that I must earnestly beg you all to come here as soon as possible. I know my dear uncle and aunt well enough to ask this without hesitation, though I have something more to request of the former. My father has gone to London with Colonel Forster to try to find her. What he means to do, I have no idea; but his extreme distress won't allow him to take the best or safest course, and Colonel Forster must be back in Brighton by tomorrow evening. In such an emergency, my uncle's advice and help would mean everything in the world; he will immediately understand what I must be feeling, and I rely on his goodness."

46.10.oldText: She burst into tears as she spoke, and for several minutes couldn't say another word. Darcy, in miserable suspense, could only murmur something indistinct about his

46.11.oldText: concern, and watch her in sympathetic silence. At last she spoke again. "I've just had a letter from Jane with such awful news. It can't be kept from anyone. My youngest sister has abandoned all her friends—has eloped—has thrown herself into the power of—of Mr. Wickham. They've run off together from Brighton. You know him too well to doubt the rest. She has no money, no connections, nothing that could tempt him to—she is lost forever."

46.13.oldText: "When I think," she added in an even more agitated voice, "that I might have prevented it! I, who knew what he was. If I had only explained some part of it—even some part of what I'd learned—to my own family! If his true character had been known, this could never have happened. But it's all, all too late now."

46.14.oldText: "I'm grieved, truly grieved," cried Darcy. "Grieved—shocked. But is it certain? Absolutely certain?"

46.15.oldText: "Oh yes! They left Brighton together on Sunday night and were traced almost to London, but not beyond. They've certainly not gone to Scotland."

46.16.oldText: "And what has been done—what has been tried—to find her?"

46.17.oldText: "My father has gone to London, and Jane has written to beg my uncle's immediate help. We'll be leaving within the half hour, I hope. But nothing can be done—I know perfectly well that nothing can be done. How can such a man be influenced? How can they even be found? I haven't the slightest hope. It's horrible in every way!"

46.18.oldText: Darcy shook his head in silent agreement.

46.19.oldText: "When my eyes were opened to his real character—oh! if I had known what I should have done, what I dared to do! But I didn't know—I was afraid of doing too much. What a wretched, wretched mistake!"

46.20.oldText: Darcy said nothing. He seemed barely to hear her, and was pacing the room in deep thought, his brow furrowed, his expression grim. Elizabeth soon noticed and instantly understood. Her influence was fading; everything must collapse under such proof of family weakness, such a guarantee of the deepest disgrace. She could neither wonder at it nor blame him; but the belief that he was giving her up brought no comfort—instead, it was precisely what made her understand her own feelings. Never had she so honestly felt that she could have loved him, as now, when all love must be in vain.

46.21.oldText: But self-pity, though it intruded, couldn't dominate. Lydia—the humiliation, the misery she was bringing on them all—soon swallowed up every private concern; and covering her face with her handkerchief, Elizabeth was soon lost to everything else. After a pause of several minutes, she was recalled to her situation only by the voice of her companion, who, in a manner that conveyed both sympathy and restraint, said—

46.22.oldText: "I'm afraid you've been wanting me to leave for some time, and I have nothing to offer as an excuse for staying except genuine, though useless, concern. Would to God that anything could be said or done on my part to offer comfort in such distress! But I won't torment you with hollow wishes that might seem like an attempt to fish for your thanks. This unfortunate affair will, I fear, prevent my sister from having the pleasure of seeing you at Pemberley today."

46.23.oldText: "Oh yes! Please apologize for us to Miss Darcy. Say that urgent business calls us home immediately. Keep the unhappy truth hidden as long as possible. I know it can't be hidden for long."

46.24.oldText: He assured her of his secrecy, expressed his sorrow for her distress once more, wished for a happier outcome than there was presently reason to hope for, and—with only one serious, lingering look—left the room.

46.25.oldText: As he went, Elizabeth felt how unlikely it was that they would ever see each other again on such friendly terms as had marked their several meetings in Derbyshire; and as she cast a look back over the whole of their acquaintance—so full of contradictions and reversals—she sighed at the perversity of feelings that now wished to continue what she had formerly been glad to see ending.

46.26.oldText: If gratitude and esteem are good foundations for affection, then Elizabeth's change of heart will seem neither unlikely nor wrong. But if otherwise—if love that springs from such sources is unreasonable or unnatural compared to what is so often described as arising at first sight, before two words have even been exchanged—then nothing can be said in her defense, except that she had given the latter method something of a trial in her partiality for Wickham, and that its failure might reasonably lead her to try the less dramatic approach. Be that as it may, she watched him go with regret; and in this early demonstration of what Lydia's scandal must produce, she found additional anguish. Not for a moment since reading Jane's second letter had she entertained any hope that Wickham meant to marry Lydia. No one but Jane, she thought, could flatter herself with such an expectation. Surprise was the least of her feelings. While the first letter's contents were still on her mind, she had been all surprise and disbelief that Wickham would marry a girl with no money. How Lydia could have attracted him had seemed incomprehensible. But now it all made too much sense. For the kind of attraction this was, she might have been appealing enough; and though Elizabeth didn't imagine Lydia had deliberately planned an elopement without intending marriage, she had no trouble believing that neither her virtue nor her judgment would protect her from becoming an easy target.

46.27.oldText: She had never noticed, while the regiment was in Hertfordshire, that Lydia had any particular interest in Wickham; but she was sure Lydia had needed only the slightest encouragement to attach herself to anyone. Sometimes one officer, sometimes another had been her favorite, as their attentions raised them in her esteem. Her affections had constantly shifted, but never without an object. The damage caused by neglect and misguided indulgence toward such a girl—oh, how painfully she felt it now!

46.28.oldText: She was wild to be home—to hear, to see, to be there to share with Jane the burdens that must now fall entirely on her, in a family so disrupted: a father gone, a mother unable to function and requiring constant care. And though she was almost certain nothing could be done for Lydia, her uncle's involvement seemed absolutely essential. Until he entered the room, the agony of waiting was severe. Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner had hurried back in alarm, assuming from the servant's account that their niece had been taken suddenly ill; but Elizabeth quickly reassured them and eagerly explained why she had sent for them, reading both letters aloud and dwelling on the postscript of the second with trembling energy. Though Lydia had never been a favorite with them, Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner couldn't help being deeply affected. Not just Lydia but the whole family was involved; and after the first exclamations of surprise and horror, Mr. Gardiner readily promised every assistance in his power. Elizabeth, though expecting nothing less, thanked him through tears of gratitude; and all three, driven by the same urgency, quickly settled everything about their journey. They would leave as soon as possible. "But what about Pemberley?" cried Mrs. Gardiner. "John told us Mr. Darcy was here when you sent for us—was that true?"

46.29.oldText: "Yes; and I told him we couldn't keep our engagement. That's all taken care of."

46.30.oldText: "What's all taken care of?" repeated her aunt as she ran to her room to pack. "And are they on such terms that she could tell him the real truth? Oh, if only I knew how things stood!"

46.31.oldText: But wishes were pointless—or at best could only distract her during the frantic hour that followed. Had Elizabeth been free to be idle, she would have been certain that all activity was impossible for someone as wretched as herself; but she had her share of tasks, and among them were notes to be written to all their friends in Lambton, with invented excuses for their sudden departure. An hour, however, saw everything done; and Mr. Gardiner, having settled the account at the inn, there was nothing left but to go. Elizabeth, after all the morning's misery, found herself in less time than she would have thought possible seated in the carriage and on the road to Longbourn.

47.2.oldText: "I do, indeed," said Mrs. Gardiner. "I'm coming around to your uncle's view. It would be too great a violation of decency, honor, and self-interest for him to be guilty of it. I can't think so badly of Wickham. Can you, Lizzy? Can you really give up on him entirely and believe him capable of it?"

47.9.oldText: "It does seem—and it's truly shocking," replied Elizabeth, with tears in her eyes, "that a sister's sense of decency and virtue should even be in question. But honestly, I don't know what to say. Perhaps I'm being unfair to her. But she's very young; she's never been taught to think about serious things; and for the last year or more, she's been given over to nothing but amusement and vanity. She's been allowed to spend her time in the most idle and frivolous way, and to adopt whatever opinions crossed her path. Since the ——shire first arrived in Meryton, nothing but love, flirtation, and officers have been in her head. She has been doing everything in her power, by thinking and talking about it constantly, to make her feelings even more—what shall I call it?—susceptible than they naturally are. And we all know that Wickham has every charm of appearance and manner that can captivate a woman."

47.11.oldText: "When does Jane ever think badly of anyone? And who is there, regardless of their past behavior, that she'd believe capable of such a thing until it was proven? But Jane knows, as well as I do, what Wickham really is. We both know he's been dishonest in every sense of the word; that he has neither integrity nor honor; that he is as false and deceitful as he is charming."

47.15.oldText: "Oh yes!—that's the worst of it. Until I went to Kent and saw so much of both Mr. Darcy and Colonel Fitzwilliam, I didn't know the truth myself. And when I got home, the ——shire was leaving Meryton in a week or two. Since that was the case, neither Jane—to whom I'd told everything—nor I thought it necessary to make our knowledge public; for what good would it apparently do anyone to destroy the favorable opinion the whole neighborhood had of him? And even when it was decided that Lydia should go with Mrs. Forster, it never occurred to me that she needed to be warned about his character. It never entered my head that she could be in any danger from his deception. That something like this would result, you can easily believe, was the farthest thing from my mind."

47.47.oldText: "Yes; but when questioned, Denny denied knowing anything about their plan and wouldn't give his real opinion about it. He didn't repeat his belief that they wouldn't marry, and from that I'm inclined to hope he was misunderstood before."

47.49.oldText: "How could such an idea have entered our minds? I felt a little uneasy—a little worried about my sister's happiness with him in marriage, because I knew his behavior hadn't always been quite right. My father and mother knew nothing of that; they only saw how imprudent such a match would be. Kitty then admitted, with obvious triumph at knowing more than the rest of us, that in Lydia's last letter she had been prepared for something like this. She had known, it turns out, about their being in love for weeks."

47.68.oldText: "I don't know; I hope not. But it's very hard to be careful at such a time. Mother was in hysterics, and though I did everything I could for her, I'm afraid I didn't do as much as I should have. The horror of what might be happening nearly overwhelmed me."

47.73.oldText: "He meant, I believe," replied Jane, "to go to Epsom, the last place where they changed horses, and try to get information from the drivers. His main goal was to find out the number of the hackney coach they took from Clapham. It had come from London with a fare, and since he thought a gentleman and lady transferring between carriages might have been noticed, he planned to make inquiries at Clapham. If he could somehow discover which house the coachman had previously dropped off his fare at, he intended to investigate there, hoping he might find the stand and number of the coach. I don't know what other plans he had; but he was in such a hurry to leave, and so distressed, that I had difficulty learning even this much."

48.11.oldText: "I feel it my duty, given our family connection and my position in life, to offer condolences on the terrible affliction you are now suffering, of which we were informed yesterday by a letter from Hertfordshire. Please be assured, my dear sir, that Mrs. Collins and I sincerely sympathize with you and all your respectable family in your present distress, which must be of the most bitter kind, since it arises from a cause that no amount of time can remedy. No argument shall be lacking on my part that might lessen so severe a misfortune, or that might comfort you in a circumstance that must be, above all others, most painful to a parent's heart. The death of your daughter would have been a blessing in comparison. And it is all the more to be lamented because there is reason to believe, as my dear Charlotte informs me, that this moral

48.12.oldText: depravity in your daughter has resulted from an excessive degree of indulgence; though, at the same time, for the comfort of yourself and Mrs. Bennet, I am inclined to think her own nature must be fundamentally bad, or she could not have been guilty of such an outrage at so young an age. However that may be, you are deeply to be pitied; an opinion shared not only by Mrs. Collins but also by Lady Catherine and her daughter, to whom I have related the matter. They agree with me that this disgraceful step by one daughter will damage the prospects of all the others; for who, as Lady Catherine herself graciously observes, would want to be connected with such a family? And this consideration leads me to reflect, with heightened satisfaction, on a certain event of last November; for had things gone otherwise, I would have been caught up in all your sorrow and disgrace. Let me advise you, then, my dear sir, to console yourself as much as possible, to cast off your unworthy child from your affection forever, and leave her to suffer the consequences of her own terrible sin.

48.14.oldText: Mr. Gardiner didn't write again until he had received a reply from Colonel Forster; and then he had nothing pleasant to report. It wasn't known that Wickham had a single relative with whom he was still in contact, and it was certain he had no close family living. His former acquaintances had been numerous, but since joining the militia he didn't appear to have been on close terms with any of them. There was no one, therefore, who could be expected to have news of him. And in the wretched state of his finances, there was a very strong motive for secrecy, in addition to his fear of being found by Lydia's family; for it had just come out that he had left gambling debts behind him to a very considerable amount. Colonel Forster believed that more than a thousand pounds would be needed to settle his expenses at Brighton. He owed a great deal in the town, but his gambling debts were even more alarming. Mr. Gardiner didn't try to hide these details from the Longbourn family. Jane heard them with horror. "A gambler!" she cried. "This is completely unexpected; I had no idea."

48.15.oldText: Mr. Gardiner added, in his letter, that they could expect to see their father home the following day, Saturday. Made spiritless by the failure of all their efforts, he had given in to his brother-in-law's urging that he return to his family and leave it to Mr. Gardiner to do whatever seemed advisable. When Mrs. Bennet was told of this, she didn't express as much satisfaction as her children expected, considering how anxious she had been about his safety.

48.16.oldText: "What! He's coming home without poor Lydia?" she cried. "Surely he won't leave London before he's found them. Who is to fight Wickham and make him marry her, if he comes away?"

48.17.oldText: Since Mrs. Gardiner wanted to get home, it was arranged that she and her children would leave for London at the same time Mr. Bennet returned. The carriage therefore took them for the first leg of their journey and brought its master back to Longbourn.

48.18.oldText: Mrs. Gardiner departed still entirely puzzled about Elizabeth and her Derbyshire friend. His name had never been voluntarily mentioned by her niece, and the vague expectation Mrs. Gardiner had formed—of a letter from him following them home—had come to nothing. Elizabeth had received no correspondence since her return that could have come from Pemberley.

48.19.oldText: The family's present unhappy state made any other explanation for her low spirits unnecessary; nothing, therefore, could be accurately guessed on that subject. Though Elizabeth—who was by now fairly well acquainted with her own feelings—was perfectly aware that, had she known nothing of Darcy, she could have borne the dread of Lydia's disgrace somewhat better. It would have spared her, she thought, one sleepless night out of two.

48.20.oldText: When Mr. Bennet arrived, he had all the appearance of his usual detached calm. He said as little as ever; made no mention of the business that had taken him away; and it was some time before his daughters had the courage to raise the subject.

48.21.oldText: It wasn't until the afternoon, when he joined them at tea, that Elizabeth ventured to bring it up; and when she briefly expressed her sorrow for what he must have endured, he replied, "Say nothing of that. Who should suffer but me? It's been my own doing, and I deserve to feel it."

48.22.oldText: "You mustn't be too hard on yourself," replied Elizabeth.

48.23.oldText: "You're right to warn me against that tendency. Human nature is so prone to it! No, Lizzy, let me for once in my life feel how much I've been to blame. I'm not afraid of being overwhelmed by the feeling. It'll pass soon enough."

48.25.oldText: "Yes; where else could they hide so well?"

48.26.oldText: "And Lydia always did want to go to London," added Kitty.

48.27.oldText: "She's happy, then," said her father drily, "and her stay there will probably be lengthy."

48.28.oldText: Then, after a short silence, he continued, "Lizzy, I bear you no grudge for being proven right in the advice you gave me last May, which—considering how things turned out—shows a certain greatness of character."

48.29.oldText: They were interrupted by Jane, who came to fetch their mother's tea.

48.30.oldText: "This is quite a production," he said. "It gives such elegance to misfortune! Another day I'll do the same: I'll sit in my library in my nightcap and dressing gown, and cause as much trouble as I can—or perhaps I'll wait until Kitty runs away."

48.31.oldText: "I'm not going to run away, Papa," said Kitty, hurt. "If I ever went to Brighton, I would behave better than Lydia."

48.32.oldText: "You go to Brighton! I wouldn't trust you within fifty miles of it! No, Kitty, I have at least learned to be cautious, and you will feel the effects of it. No officer is ever to enter my house again, or even pass through the village. Balls will be absolutely forbidden unless you dance with one of your sisters. And you're never to set foot outside the door until you can prove you've spent ten minutes of every day doing something sensible."

48.33.oldText: Kitty, who took all these threats seriously, began to cry.

48.34.oldText: "Well, well," he said, "don't make yourself miserable. If you're a good girl for the next ten years, I'll take you to a military review at the end of them."

49.3.oldText: The girls ran off, too excited to speak. They ran through the hall into the breakfast room; from there to the library—their father was in neither; and they were about to look for him upstairs when they were met by the butler, who said—

49.17.oldText: Elizabeth read on: "I have seen them both. They are not married, nor can I find there was ever any intention of it; but if you are willing to honor the commitments I have ventured to make on your behalf, I hope it will not be long before they are. All that is required of you is to guarantee your daughter, by legal settlement, her equal share of the five thousand pounds secured among your children after the death of yourself and my sister; and moreover, to commit to allowing her, during your lifetime, one hundred pounds per year. These are conditions which, considering everything, I had no hesitation in agreeing to, as far as I felt authorized. I shall send this by express so that no time is lost in getting your reply. You will easily understand from these details that Mr. Wickham's financial situation is not so hopeless as generally believed. The world has been deceived on that point; and I am happy to say there will be some money remaining, even after all his debts are cleared, to settle on my niece in addition to her own share. If, as I expect, you send me full authority to act on your behalf throughout this matter, I will immediately instruct Haggerston to prepare a proper settlement. There will be no need whatever for you to come to London again; so stay quietly at Longbourn and trust in my diligence and care. Send your reply as soon as you can, and make sure to write clearly. We have judged it best that my niece be married from this house, which I hope you will approve. She comes to us today. I shall write again as soon as anything more is settled. Yours, etc.

49.41.oldText: "We must try to forget everything that's happened on either side," said Jane. "I hope and trust they will be happy. His agreeing to marry her is proof, I want to believe, that he's come to see things differently. Their love for each other will give them stability; and I flatter myself they will settle down quietly and live so sensibly that in time their past recklessness will be forgotten."

50.3.oldText: Five thousand pounds had been settled on Mrs. Bennet and the children by the marriage agreement. But how it should be divided among the children depended on the parents' wishes. This was one point that now needed to be settled regarding Lydia at least, and Mr. Bennet had no hesitation in accepting the proposal before him. In terms of grateful acknowledgment for his brother's kindness, though expressed as briefly as possible, he then set down on paper his complete approval of everything that had been done and his willingness to fulfill the commitments made on his behalf. He had never imagined that, if Wickham could be persuaded to marry his daughter, it would be done with so little inconvenience to himself as the current arrangement required. He would be scarcely ten pounds a year worse off by the hundred that was to be paid them; for, what with her room and board, her pocket money, and the constant gifts of cash that passed to her through her mother, Lydia's expenses had always nearly reached that amount.

50.8.oldText: Her husband let her talk on without interruption while the servants were present. But when they had left, he said, "Mrs. Bennet, before you claim any or all of these houses for your son and daughter, let us understand each other. They will never be admitted into any house in this neighborhood. I will not encourage the recklessness of either of them by receiving them at Longbourn."

50.9.oldText: A long argument followed this declaration, but Mr. Bennet was firm. It soon led to another dispute; and Mrs. Bennet discovered, with amazement and horror, that her husband would not contribute a single penny toward buying clothes for his daughter. He insisted she would receive from him no token of affection whatever on this occasion. Mrs. Bennet could hardly believe it. That his anger could reach such a point of unimaginable stubbornness as to deny his daughter a privilege without which her marriage would hardly seem real exceeded everything she thought possible. She was more upset about the disgrace that a lack of new clothes would bring to her daughter's wedding than by any shame over the elopement or the weeks of living with Wickham before the ceremony.

50.11.oldText: She had no fear of the secret spreading through him. There were few people whose discretion she would have trusted more; but at the same time there was no one whose knowledge of a sister's downfall would have mortified her so deeply. Not, however, from any fear of personal harm to herself; for in any case there seemed to be an impassable gulf between them. Had Lydia's marriage been concluded on the most honorable terms, Mr. Darcy would surely never connect himself with a family to whose existing objections would now be added an alliance with the man he most justly despised.

50.18.oldText: "It was very much my wish that he should do so," he added, "as soon as the marriage was settled. And I think you'll agree that a move from that regiment is highly advisable for both his sake and my niece's. It is Mr. Wickham's intention to join the Regular Army; and among his former friends there are still some able and willing to assist him. He has the promise of a commission in General ——'s regiment, now stationed in the north. It's an advantage to have it so far from this part of the country. He gives fair promises; and I hope that among different people, where they each have a reputation to maintain, they will both be more sensible. I have written to Colonel Forster to inform him of our arrangements and to ask him to settle Wickham's various debts in and near Brighton, for which I have pledged myself. And would you take the trouble to make similar assurances to his creditors in Meryton, of whom I am enclosing a list based on his information? He has declared all his debts; I hope at least he hasn't deceived us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything will be completed within a week. They will then join his regiment, unless they are first invited to Longbourn; and I understand from Mrs. Gardiner that my niece very much wants to see you all before she leaves the south. She is well, and sends her dutiful regards to you and her mother.—Yours, etc.

50.22.oldText: His daughter's request—for such it might be considered—to be welcomed back into the family before heading north was initially met with a flat refusal. But Jane and Elizabeth, who agreed that for their sister's sake and dignity she should be acknowledged by her parents on her marriage, urged him so earnestly yet so reasonably to receive her and her husband at Longbourn as soon as they were married, that he was eventually persuaded. And their mother had the satisfaction of knowing she would be able to show off her married daughter in the neighborhood before she was banished to the north. When Mr. Bennet wrote again to his brother, therefore, he sent his permission for them to come; and it was settled that, as soon as the ceremony was over, they would proceed to Longbourn. Elizabeth was surprised, however, that Wickham would agree to such a plan; and had she consulted only her own wishes, seeing him again would have been the last thing she wanted.

51.3.oldText: Their reception from Mr. Bennet, to whom they then turned, was not nearly as warm. His expression actually grew more stern, and he barely opened his mouth. The brazen confidence of the young couple was, in fact, enough to provoke him.

51.35.oldText: With such an encouragement to ask, Elizabeth was forced to put it out of her power by walking away.

52.3.oldText: "I have just received your letter and shall devote this entire morning to answering it, since I foresee that a little writing won't cover what I have to tell you. I must say I'm surprised by your question; I didn't expect it from you. But don't think me angry—I only mean to let you know I hadn't imagined such inquiries would be necessary on your side. If you genuinely don't understand me, forgive my frankness. Your uncle is as surprised as I am; and nothing but the belief that you were personally involved would have allowed him to act as he did. But if you truly are innocent and uninformed, I must be more explicit. On the very day I returned home from Longbourn, your uncle had a most unexpected visitor. Mr. Darcy called and was closeted with him for several hours. It was all over before I arrived, so my curiosity wasn't quite as horribly tested as yours seems to have been. He came to tell Mr. Gardiner that he had discovered where your sister and Mr. Wickham were, and that he had seen and spoken with them both—Wickham repeatedly, Lydia once. From what I can gather, he left Derbyshire only one day after we did, and came to London determined to find them. His stated reason was his conviction that Wickham's worthlessness had not been made known widely enough to prevent any young woman of good character from trusting him. He generously blamed the whole situation on his own mistaken pride, and confessed that he had previously thought it beneath him to make his private dealings public. His character, he felt, should speak for itself. He therefore called it his duty to step forward and try to remedy a problem he had helped to create. If he had another motive, I'm sure it would do him no discredit. He had been in London several days before he could find them, but he had a lead that we lacked, and knowing this was another reason he resolved to follow us. There was a woman, it seems—a Mrs. Younge—who had once been Miss Darcy's governess and was dismissed for some reason he didn't specify. She had taken a large house in Edward Street and was making her living by letting rooms. This Mrs. Younge was, he knew, closely connected with Wickham, and he went to her for information as soon as he arrived in London. But it was two or three days before he could get what he needed from her. She wouldn't betray her friend, I suppose, without being bribed, since she really did know where he was. Wickham had gone to her on their first arrival in London, and had she been able to take them in, they would have stayed with her. At last, however, our kind friend obtained the address. They were in —— Street. He saw Wickham, and then insisted on seeing Lydia. His first aim, he admitted, was to persuade her to leave her current disgraceful situation and return to her family, offering his help as far as it could go. But he found Lydia absolutely determined to stay. She cared nothing for any of her friends; she wanted no help from him; she refused to hear of leaving Wickham. She was sure they'd be married sooner or later, and it didn't much matter when. Since those were her feelings, the only option, he felt, was to secure and expedite a marriage which—as he easily learned from his very first conversation with Wickham—had never been Wickham's intention. Wickham admitted he'd been forced to leave the regiment because of pressing debts of honor, and didn't hesitate to blame the entire mess on Lydia's foolishness alone. He intended to resign his commission immediately; as for his future, he could guess very little. He had to go somewhere, but didn't know where, and knew he'd have nothing to live on. Mr. Darcy asked why he didn't simply marry Lydia. Though Mr. Bennet wasn't thought to be wealthy, he could have done something for his son-in-law, and Wickham's situation could only have been improved by marriage. But in response, Wickham revealed he still hoped to make his fortune through a more advantageous marriage elsewhere. Under the circumstances, however, he wasn't likely to resist the temptation of immediate relief. They met several times, as there was much to negotiate. Wickham naturally wanted more than he could get, but was eventually brought to see reason. Once everything was settled between them, Mr. Darcy's next step was to inform your uncle, and he first called at Gracechurch Street the evening before I came home. But Mr. Gardiner wasn't available, and Mr. Darcy learned that your father was still with him but would leave London the next morning. He didn't think your father was the right person to consult, preferring your uncle, and therefore easily delayed the meeting until after your father's departure. He didn't leave his name, and until the next day it was only known that a gentleman had called on business. On Saturday he came again. Your father was gone, your uncle was home, and, as I said before, they had a great deal to discuss. They met again on Sunday, and then I saw him too. It wasn't all settled until Monday; as soon as it was, the express was sent to Longbourn. But our visitor was very stubborn. I suspect, Lizzy, that stubbornness is the real fault in his character. He has been accused of many things at different times, but this is the true one. Nothing was to be done that he didn't do himself; though I'm sure (and I don't say this to be thanked, so please say nothing about it) your uncle would have been perfectly willing to handle the whole thing. They argued about it for a long time, longer than either the gentleman or lady concerned deserved. But at last your uncle was forced to give in, and instead of being allowed to help his niece, had to settle for merely getting the credit for it—which went very much against the grain. I truly believe your letter this morning gave him great pleasure, because it called for an explanation that would strip him of his borrowed glory and give the praise where it was due. But, Lizzy, this must go no further than yourself, or Jane at most. You know fairly well, I suppose, what has been done for the young people. His debts are to be paid—amounting, I believe, to considerably more than a thousand pounds—another thousand in addition to her own share settled on her, and his commission purchased. The reason all this was to be done by him alone is what I've described above. It was owing to him, to his reticence and lack of proper openness, that Wickham's character had been so misunderstood, and consequently that he had been received and welcomed as he was. Perhaps there's some truth in this, though I doubt whether his reserve, or anyone's reserve, can truly be held responsible for what happened. But in spite of all this noble talk, my dear Lizzy, you may rest perfectly assured that your uncle would never have given in if we hadn't credited him with another interest in the affair. When all this was resolved, Mr. Darcy returned to his friends at Pemberley; but it was agreed he would be in London again when the wedding took place, and all financial matters were to be finalized then. I believe I've now told you everything. It is a story which you tell me will greatly surprise you; I hope at least it won't displease you. Lydia came to us, and Wickham was a constant visitor. He was exactly as he'd been when I knew him in Hertfordshire; but I won't tell you how little I was satisfied with her behavior while she stayed with us, except that I saw from Jane's letter last Wednesday that her conduct since returning home has been equally bad, so what I say now can't cause you any fresh pain. I spoke to her repeatedly in the most serious way, pointing out the wickedness of what she'd done and all the unhappiness she'd brought on her family. If she heard me, it was by luck, because I'm sure she wasn't listening. I was sometimes quite exasperated; but then I remembered my dear Elizabeth and Jane, and for their sakes I was patient. Mr. Darcy was punctual in his return and, as Lydia told you, attended the wedding. He dined with us the following day and was to leave London again on Wednesday or Thursday. Will you be very angry with me, my dear Lizzy, if I take this opportunity to say (what I was never brave enough to say before) how much I like him? His behavior toward us has been, in every way, as pleasing as it was in Derbyshire. His intelligence and opinions all appeal to me; he needs only a little more liveliness, and that, if he marries wisely, his wife may teach him. I thought him very reserved; he hardly ever mentioned your name. But reserve seems to be the fashion. Please forgive me if I've been too forward, or at least don't punish me by banning me from Pemberley. I'll never be quite happy until I've been all around the park. A low carriage with a nice little pair of ponies would be the very thing. But I must stop writing. The children have been wanting me for the last half hour.

52.14.oldText: "I almost envy you the experience, and yet I think it would be too much for me—though I could take it in on my way to Newcastle. And you saw the old housekeeper, I suppose? Poor Reynolds—she was always very fond of me. But of course she didn't mention my name to you."

52.29.oldText: "I mention it because that's the living I ought to have had. A most delightful place! Excellent rectory house! It would have suited me in every way."

52.32.oldText: "I did hear, from a source I considered just as reliable, that the living was left to you only conditionally, at the discretion of the current patron."

52.35.oldText: "You did! And there was not no truth in that. You may remember what I told you about it when we first discussed it."

53.17.oldText: Elizabeth didn't know what to make of it. Had she not seen him in Derbyshire, she might have supposed he was coming with no intention beyond what was openly stated; but she still thought him attracted to Jane, and wavered between thinking he was coming with his friend's permission or being bold enough to come without it.

53.26.oldText: Consoled by this plan, she was better able to bear her husband's rudeness; though it was very annoying to know that her neighbors might all see Mr. Bingley before they did. As the day of his arrival drew near—

53.39.oldText: Elizabeth said as little to either of them as politeness allowed and sat down again to her work, with an intensity she didn't usually show. She had ventured only one glance at Darcy. He looked serious as usual—more like his old Hertfordshire manner, she thought, than how he'd been at Pemberley. But perhaps he couldn't be the same in her mother's house as before her uncle and aunt. It was a painful thought, but not an unlikely one.

53.48.oldText: "I was starting to think you'd never come back. People did say you meant to leave the place entirely at Michaelmas; but I hope that's not true. A great many changes have happened in the neighborhood since you left. Miss Lucas is married and settled, and one of my own daughters too. I suppose you've heard of it; you must have seen it in the papers. It was in the Times and the Courier, I know; though it wasn't printed as it ought to have been. It only said, 'Lately, George Wickham, Esq., to Miss Lydia Bennet,' without a syllable about her father, or where she lived, or anything. It was my brother Gardiner's work, and I wonder how he made such a mess of it. Did you see it?"

54.10.oldText: On Tuesday a large party gathered at Longbourn; and the two who were most anxiously awaited arrived, to the credit of their punctuality as sportsmen, in very good time. When they moved to the dining room, Elizabeth eagerly watched to see whether Bingley would take the seat that, at all their previous parties, had been next to her sister. Her calculating mother had the same idea and refrained from inviting him to sit by herself. On entering the room, he seemed to hesitate; but Jane happened to look around and happened to smile; and that decided it. He sat down beside her.

54.11.oldText: Elizabeth, with a triumphant feeling, looked toward his friend. He appeared nobly indifferent; and she would have imagined Bingley had received Darcy's blessing to be happy, had she not seen his eyes also turn toward Mr. Darcy with an expression of half-amused alarm.

54.13.oldText: She hoped the evening would provide some chance to bring them together—that the entire visit wouldn't pass without something more than the polite greeting that had accompanied his entrance. Anxious and restless, the period in the drawing room before the gentlemen arrived was tedious and dull to a degree that almost made her rude. She looked forward to their entrance as the moment on which all her chances of enjoying the evening depended.

54.18.oldText: "A man who has already been refused! How could I ever be foolish enough to expect a renewed proposal? Is there a man alive who wouldn't resist the indignity of proposing twice to the same woman? There is no insult more offensive to their pride."

55.17.oldText: Mrs. Bennet's plans for that day failed. Bingley was everything that was charming, except the declared lover of her daughter. His ease and cheerfulness made him a most agreeable addition to the evening; and he endured the mother's heavy-handed interference and heard all her foolish remarks with a patience and composure particularly grateful to the daughter.

55.19.oldText: After this day, Jane said no more about her indifference. Not a word passed between the sisters about Bingley; but Elizabeth went to bed happily certain that everything must soon be settled, unless Mr. Darcy returned later than planned. She did seriously believe, however, that all this must be happening with that gentleman's approval.

55.20.oldText: Bingley was punctual to his appointment; and he and Mr. Bennet spent the morning together as agreed. The latter was much more agreeable than his companion had expected. There was nothing foolish or presumptuous about Bingley to provoke his ridicule or put him off; and he was more talkative and less eccentric than Mr. Bennet had ever seen him. Bingley naturally returned with him to dinner; and in the evening Mrs. Bennet's ingenuity was again at work clearing everyone from the room. Elizabeth, who had a letter to write, went to the breakfast room for that purpose soon after tea; for since the others were all going to play cards, she wouldn't be missed to counteract her mother's plots.

55.21.oldText: But when she returned to the drawing room, her letter finished, she saw, to her astonishment, that there was reason to fear her mother had been too clever for her own good. Opening the door, she found her sister and Bingley standing together by the fireplace, clearly in the middle of an earnest conversation; and had this not been enough to arouse suspicion, the faces of both, as they hastily turned and moved apart, would have told everything. Their situation was awkward enough; but hers, she felt, was worse. Not a word was spoken by either; and Elizabeth was about to leave again when Bingley, who like the others had sat down, suddenly stood, whispered a few words to her sister, and rushed from the room.

55.46.oldText: "It must have been his sisters' doing. They certainly didn't encourage his acquaintance with me, which I can't wonder at, since he could have chosen so much more advantageously. But when they see, as I trust they will, that their brother is happy with me, they'll learn to accept it, and we'll be on good terms again—though we can never be what we once were."

56.1.oldText: They were all prepared to be surprised, but their astonishment exceeded all expectations; and on the part of Mrs. Bennet and Kitty—though they had never met her—it was even greater than Elizabeth's.

56.12.oldText: "May I ask whether you left Mr. and Mrs. Collins well?"

56.16.oldText: "Miss Bennet, there seemed to be a rather pretty little wilderness on one side of your lawn. I should like to take a turn in it, if you will come with me."

56.45.oldText: "These are heavy punishments," replied Elizabeth. "But the wife of Mr. Darcy must have such extraordinary advantages attached to her position that, on the whole, she would have no cause for complaint."

56.47.oldText: "That will make your Ladyship's current situation all the more unpleasant; but it will have no effect on me."

56.50.oldText: "True. You are a gentleman's daughter. But who was your mother? Who are your uncles and aunts? Do not imagine me ignorant of their situation."

56.61.oldText: "You can now have nothing further to say," she answered angrily. "You have insulted me in every possible way. I must ask to return to the house."

56.73.oldText: "She didn't want to," said her daughter. "She had to go."

57.4.oldText: The surprise of the rest of the family at learning who their visitor had been was considerable; but they satisfied their curiosity with the same kind of explanation that had appeased Mrs. Bennet, and Elizabeth was spared much questioning on the subject.

57.13.oldText: "Something very much to the point, naturally. He begins with congratulations on the approaching marriage of my eldest daughter, which he has apparently heard about from the helpful, gossiping Lucases. I won't bore you by reading what he says about that. What concerns you is this: 'Having offered you the sincere congratulations of Mrs. Collins and myself on this happy event, let me add a brief note on another subject, of which we have been informed by the same source. Your daughter Elizabeth, it is presumed, will not long bear the name of Bennet after her elder sister has given it up; and the chosen partner of her fate may reasonably be looked up to as one of the most distinguished personages in this land.' Can you possibly guess, Lizzy, who is meant? 'This young gentleman is blessed, in a special way, with everything the heart of mortal can most desire—magnificent property, noble family, and powerful connections. Yet, despite all these enticements, let me warn my cousin Elizabeth, and yourself, of the dangers you may face by too hastily accepting this gentleman's proposals, which you will of course be eager to do.' Have you any idea, Lizzy, who this gentleman is? But now it comes out. 'My reason for cautioning you is as follows: we have reason to believe that his aunt, Lady Catherine de Bourgh, does not look on the match with a friendly eye.' Mr. Darcy, you see, is the man! Now, Lizzy, I think I have surprised you. Could he, or the Lucases, have picked any man in our entire circle of acquaintance whose name would have more completely contradicted what they claimed? Mr. Darcy, who never looks at any woman except to find a flaw, and who probably never looked at you in his life! It's priceless!"

57.19.oldText: "Yes, that's what makes it funny. Had they picked any other man it would have been nothing; but his perfect indifference and your open dislike make it so delightfully absurd! Much as I hate writing, I wouldn't give up Mr. Collins's correspondence for anything. In fact, when I read one of his letters, I almost prefer him to Wickham, much as I value my son-in-law's shamelessness and hypocrisy. And tell me, Lizzy, what did Lady Catherine say about this report? Did she come to withhold her consent?"

58.0.oldText: Instead of receiving the expected excuses from his friend, Bingley was able to bring Darcy with him to Longbourn only a few days after Lady Catherine's visit. The gentlemen arrived early, and before Mrs. Bennet had time to mention having seen his aunt—something Elizabeth dreaded every moment—Bingley, wanting to be alone with Jane, suggested they all go for a walk. It was agreed. Mrs. Bennet never walked; Mary could never spare the time; but the remaining five set off together. Bingley and Jane soon fell behind, while Elizabeth, Kitty, and Darcy were left to entertain each other. Very little was said by any of them; Kitty was too afraid of Darcy to talk; Elizabeth was secretly forming a desperate resolution; and perhaps he was doing the same.

58.8.oldText: They walked on without knowing which direction they were going. There was too much to think, feel, and say for them to notice anything else. She soon learned that they owed their present understanding to the efforts of his aunt, who had indeed called on him on her way back through London, and told him about her visit to Longbourn—its purpose and the substance of her conversation with Elizabeth—dwelling on every word of the latter which, in her Ladyship's view, showed particular defiance and audacity, in the belief that such a report would help her obtain from her nephew the promise Elizabeth had refused to give. But, unfortunately for her Ladyship, the effect had been exactly the opposite.

58.12.oldText: "We will not quarrel over who bears more blame for that evening," said Elizabeth. "Neither of us, strictly examined, behaved well; but since then we have both, I hope, improved in civility."

58.13.oldText: "I cannot be so easily reconciled to myself. The memory of what I said—my conduct, my manners, my words during that whole scene—has been, and remains, unbearably painful. Your rebuke, so justly delivered, I shall never forget: 'Had you behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner.' Those were your words. You cannot imagine how they have tortured me—though I admit it was some time before I was reasonable enough to accept their justice."

58.23.oldText: "I can't credit you with any such philosophy. Your memories must be so free of self-reproach that the contentment they bring comes not from philosophy but, what is far better, from innocence. But for me, it's not so. Painful memories will intrude, and they cannot and should not be pushed away. I have been a selfish man all my life, in practice though not in principle. As a child I was taught what was right, but I was not taught to correct my temperament. I was given good principles but left to follow them with pride and arrogance. Unfortunately, as an only son—for many years an only child—I was spoiled by my parents, who, though good people themselves (my father especially, as kind and generous as anyone), allowed, encouraged, almost taught me to be selfish and domineering, to care for no one outside my own family circle, to think poorly of the rest of the world—to wish, at least, to think poorly of their intelligence and worth compared with my own. Such I was from eight to twenty-eight; and such I might still be, but for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! What do I not owe you! You taught me a lesson, hard at first but invaluable. By you I was properly humbled. I came to you without a doubt that I would be accepted. You showed me how completely inadequate were all my claims to please a woman worth pleasing."

59.10.oldText: "Very, very much. Nothing could give Bingley or me more delight. But we had considered it impossible—we had even discussed it. And do you really love him enough? Oh, Lizzy! Do anything rather than marry without love. Are you quite sure you feel what you should?"

59.26.oldText: During their walk, it was decided that Mr. Bennet's consent should be sought that evening. Elizabeth reserved her mother's reaction for herself. She couldn't predict how her mother would take it—sometimes doubting whether all his wealth and status would be enough to overcome her dislike of the man; but whether she was violently opposed or violently delighted, her manner would be equally unsuitable. Elizabeth could no more bear to have Mr. Darcy witness the first outburst of her mother's joy than the first blast of her disapproval.

59.34.oldText: "Lizzy," said her father, "I have given him my consent. He is the kind of man to whom I could never dare refuse anything he asked. I now give my consent to you, if you are determined to have him. But let me advise you to think carefully. I know your nature, Lizzy. I know you could be neither happy nor respectable unless you truly respected your husband—unless you looked up to him. Your lively mind would put you in the greatest danger in an unequal marriage. You could scarcely escape unhappiness and disgrace. My child, do not let me suffer the grief of seeing you unable to respect your partner in life. You don't know what you're doing."

60.27.oldText: Before any reply could come from Mr. Collins, or any congratulations to Elizabeth from his wife, the Longbourn family heard that the Collinses had come to Lucas Lodge in person. The reason for this sudden move was soon clear. Lady Catherine had been made so furious by her nephew's letter that Charlotte, who was genuinely happy about the match, wanted to get away until the storm blew over. At such a moment, the arrival of her friend was a real pleasure to Elizabeth; though in the course of their meetings she sometimes felt the pleasure was dearly bought, seeing Mr. Darcy subjected to all the fawning and obsequious politeness of her husband. He bore it, however, with remarkable calm. He could even listen to Sir William Lucas complimenting him on carrying off the brightest jewel of the county, and expressing hopes of their all meeting frequently at St. James's, with very decent composure. If he did shrug his shoulders, it wasn't until Sir William was out of sight.

61.4.oldText: Mary was the only daughter who remained at home; and she was necessarily drawn away from her books by Mrs. Bennet's inability to sit alone. Mary was forced to mix more with society, but she could still moralize over every morning call; and since she was no longer humiliated by comparisons between her sisters' beauty and her own, it was suspected by her father that she accepted the change without much reluctance.

61.5.oldText: As for Wickham and Lydia, their characters suffered no transformation from her sisters' marriages. He bore with philosophical calm the certainty that Elizabeth must now learn of all his ingratitude and dishonesty that had previously been unknown to her; and despite everything, he was not entirely without hope that Darcy might still be persuaded to advance his career. The congratulatory letter Elizabeth received from Lydia on her marriage showed that, by his wife at least if not by himself, such a hope was alive. The letter went like this:

61.9.oldText: As it happened, Elizabeth very much would rather not, and she tried in her reply to put an end to every such appeal. Such relief as she could provide, however, through careful economy in her own private spending, she frequently sent them. It had always been obvious that an income like theirs, managed by two people so extravagant and careless about the future, must be woefully insufficient; and whenever they moved, either Jane or Elizabeth could be sure of being asked for some small help in paying their bills. Their way of life, even after peace was restored and they were settled in a home, was thoroughly unstable. They were always moving from place to place in search of a cheap situation, and always spending more than they should. His affection for her soon faded into indifference; hers lasted a little longer; and despite her youth and her behavior, she retained all the social standing that marriage had given her. Though Darcy would never receive Wickham at Pemberley, he helped him further in his career, for Elizabeth's sake. Lydia was an occasional visitor when her husband was off enjoying himself in London or Bath; and with the Bingleys they both frequently stayed so long that even Bingley's good nature was strained, and he went so far as to talk of hinting they should leave.

61.11.oldText: Pemberley was now Georgiana's home, and the bond between the two sisters was exactly what Darcy had hoped to see. They were able to love each other as well as they had intended. Georgiana had the highest opinion in the world of Elizabeth; though at first she was often startled to the point of alarm by her lively, playful way of talking to her brother. He, who had always inspired in Georgiana a respect that almost overpowered her affection, was now the target of open teasing. Her mind received a lesson it had never encountered before. Through Elizabeth's example, she began to understand that a woman may take liberties with her husband that a brother will not always tolerate from a much younger sister.

61.12.oldText: Lady Catherine was extremely indignant at her nephew's marriage; and since she gave free rein to all the genuine frankness of her character in her reply to the letter announcing the engagement, she used language so abusive—especially of Elizabeth—that all communication between them ceased for some time. But at last, through Elizabeth's persuasion, he was brought to overlook the insult and seek a reconciliation; and after a little further resistance, his aunt gave way, either from affection for him or curiosity to see how his wife conducted herself. She even condescended to visit them at Pemberley, despite the pollution its woods had received not merely from the presence of such a mistress but from the visits of her uncle and aunt from the city.
